#3357. Apple @ Work: Next to a growing token bill, Macs might start looking like a bargain

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple hardware costs more than it did a year ago, and if you have purchased a fleet recently, you are feeling it. Now, one thing I should mention: Macs have not risen in price with inflation or performance. If you think about what a Mac mini or MacBook Air cost when they launched vs. today, I would still say they are extremely affordable. With that being said, there’s a scenario taking shape in the enterprise where the price of a Mac matters a lot less than it used to. If open-weight AI models become a real part of how companies work, Apple Silicon might end up looking basically free compared to the token bill it supplements.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Cloud AI in the enterprise is priced by the token, and that’s a fine model when usage is moderate. The problem is that usage isn’t staying light. Agentic tools that write code, analyze documents, and run multistep tasks consume tokens at a pace a chatbot never did, and the bill scales right along with them. Earlier this year, Fleet’s IT leadership research cited a company that burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in four months after rolling an AI coding tool out to roughly 5,000 engineers. That’s the risk with a variable cost by token usage. Finance is somewhat in the dark on what the number is until the invoice shows up.

Local hardware works the opposite way, where you pay once, and the cost is capped. Every hour that machine spends running a model after that costs you very little, aside from power usage.

Someone I’ve long respected, Horace Dediu, showed some interesting numbers in a recent Asymco piece that really shows the opportunity ahead for Apple. In one example, a 26-billion-parameter model used for analysis four hours a day, around 150 million tokens a month, runs $450 to $850 per user per month through a cloud provider. A 16″ MacBook Pro with an M5 Max and 128GB of unified memory costs about $6,500 and can run a model locally. That’s a payback period of 7 to 14 months. He gives a lot more examples, and it’s worth a read to see Apple’s opportunity here.

The reason Apple Silicon is so well suited to this is unified memory. On most PCs, the GPU has its own small memory pool, and the model has to fit within it. On Apple Silicon, the GPU shares the entire memory pool, so a laptop with 128GB can hold a model that would need a far more expensive setup elsewhere.

Viewed through this lens, a price increase on a Mac Studio is a rounding error. If the machine pays for itself in under a year, and Apple Silicon Macs can stay in service for four to five years, it’s practically free over a normal refresh cycle. Now, if agentic coding keeps improving at such a rapid pace, you might end up upgrading sooner than that.

All of this hinges on one assumption: the math only works if an open-weight model running locally is good enough for your task day-to-day. For a lot of everyday work, like summarizing docs, drafting, content analysis on internal data, and basic routine coding, the gap between open-weight models and the frontier has narrowed significantly recently. For the hardest reasoning and coding tasks, frontier models still lead, and that isn’t changing anytime soon.

There are other caveats, too: his usage figures in those examples are high, and a typical employee isn’t burning through 150 million tokens a month. Token prices have also been falling, narrowing the gap over time. I am really interested in a hybrid model as well. Cribl recently launched StreamAI, an AI gateway for telemetry that routes each prompt to the right model and includes built-in budget control. At JNUC 2026, Jamf showed on-device AI support that deploys models through blueprints, routes prompts through an on-device AI gateway, and governs all of it with AI policies. Apple is clearly thinking about this too. At JNUC, Apple’s Jeremy Butcher had this to say regarding cloud and on-device AI:

“We think our platform makes for the best way to do both,” said Butcher. “We continue to have these conversations, and we look forward to working with all of you to bring it to life.”

A hybrid model might be the best of both worlds, with routine work running locally and the hardest tasks routed to frontier models in the cloud. Either way, Apple is well positioned. Even with RAM and GPU shortages driving up hardware prices, the ROI on Apple Silicon looks promising if open-weight models end up handling a decent share of enterprise AI workloads. Mac prices are going up, but token bills are going up faster (even if token prices continue to fall).

#3356. The Best Gifts for Music Lovers, According to Our Editors

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

Shopping for music lovers isn’t an easy task. Music obsessives have a penchant for snobbery, which can make them some of the most difficult giftees to shop for come holiday season. Luckily for us here at Rolling Stone, music lovers are everywhere. And luckily for everyone else, we also know how to find the best gifts for music lovers.

To help find the best gifts, we had our staff of music-obsessed shopping editors round up gifts that any music nerd in your life will not just appreciate this holiday, but actually use throughout 2027 and beyond. These run the gamut from affordable custom wall art and earplugs to the latest and greatest headphones if you’re really looking to treat the music lover in your life.

Ahead are the best gifts for music lovers during the 2026 holiday season.

One of the safest gift ideas for music lovers (and almost anyone else, for that matter) is a gift card to StubHub, which will let them see the show of their choice for less. You can go low to help offset the ludicrous ticket prices we’re now used to, or go high if you really want to cover a whole show.

Earplugs are a must for anyone attending shows regularly, and Loop has become the industry go-to. Options like these Experience 2 earplugs work to lower the volume of live music while retaining all the detail, keeping ears safe while letting the wearer enjoy the show as normal.

DJ controllers are the new guitars. If you have an aspiring DJ on your list — or anyone who likes to host parties — they’ll be thrilled to unwrap this Pioneer DJ DDJ-FLX4. The entry-level controller is a great introduction to the technology, and it’s relatively affordable as far as music gear goes.

This Is Your Brain on Music: The Science of a Human Obsession has been out for two decades, but it’s still one of the best reads for anyone interested in the art. Written by neuroscientist, musician, and record producer Daniel J. Levitin, the book explores how we hear music and why it moves us.

If you know a song that your giftee loves, this wall art is a thoughtful gift. It presents the song lyrics as a vinyl record, and the whole design is minimal and tasteful enough to fit most interior decor looks. You also get several size and frame options to choose from.

For guitar players, pick up one of these customizable straps. They’re made using soft calf leather, and your message is engraved (instead of painted or printed on). Besides the actual message, you’ll be able to choose the font and the position, and you can even add a photo.

An easy, affordable gift for music lovers (or white elephant parties) is these cute record coasters. They’re made of vinyl to feel like the real thing and feature unique album covers on each one in the pack of six.

Sonos’ new Play speaker bridges the gap between a home device and a portable, offering great sound everywhere. This makes it ideal for college students and recent grads setting up a first apartment.

One of the best pairs of headphones to come out this past year is Technics’ A1000. The cans are based around an advanced 40mm Magnetic Fluid Driver that produces the kind of crisp, natural sound audiophiles will appreciate.

A mini karaoke machine like this one can turn any hangout into a party. The little machine includes two microphones and surprisingly loud sound for its size.

If you’re shopping for a music lover who’s also a sports fan, this summer’s Grateful Dead x Knicks merch is a slam dunk.

A subscription to Fender Play is a great choice for aspiring guitar players. The online learning platform helps beginner and intermediate players improve through high-quality, bite-size videos and exercises.

A subscription to the authority on music and culture is a great gift for anyone. And no, we’re not biased.

Vinyl has been back for a while now, and brands are putting out some very cool record players, including ones with reasonable price tags. Our favorite budget-friendly record player — which also makes a great gift — is this unique Sound Burger from Audio-Technica.

CD players also made a comeback recently. Luckily for us gifters, there are some very fun, affordable options out there, like this colorful player from Gueray.

If your giftee plays music at home (especially drums) or just likes their speakers loud, these acoustic wall panels will let them do it without disturbing others.

One of the best music-book releases of the year was Liza Minnelli’s autobiography, Kids, Wait Till You Hear This! The book gives readers a look at the EGOT winner’s life and career, including her Hollywood upbringing and reflections at nearly 80 years old.

#3355. Apple Maps begins blurring NASA, Space Force, and Air Force bases

You’re not a real space or aviation nerd unless you’ve taken to a map service and zoomed on the historic NASA launch pads or your local Air Force Bases, just for fun, you know? However, a recent change to Apple Maps now has some of those locations blurred from view, blocking anyone from seeing fighters on tarmacs or rockets on launch pads.

It probably makes sense as a reasonable security measure, why should some of the most sensitive locations to the United States be easily seen from commercial services on anyone’s phone?

Not every base we’ve checked has been blurred. Some rather large US Navy installations like Pearl Harbor, Norfolk, and Naval Station Great Lakes are left unburied. As a Wisconsin resident, I checked my local Air National Guard bases, those two have been left clear to see.

What we have discovered are now blurred are a lot of NASA and US Space Force locations, including Wallops Flight Facility, Virginia, Stennis Space Center, Mississippi, Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and Vandenberg Space Force Base, California.

This change looks to have been rather recent, with no announcement by Apple for the change. On the contrary, Google Maps, has not blurred any of these military locations. It is presumed that Apple will continue to role out blurred map changes to more bases in the future.

Apple’s choice for which locations to blur first is interesting. Whiteman Air Force Base, the location of the bulk of the Air Force’s B2 stealth bombers, capable of carrying nuclear weapons, is logically blurred from view. Ellsworth Air Force Base, one of two state-side homes of the B-1B stealth bomber, both nuclear capable and can carry the most payload than any other US bomber, is also blurred. However, Dyess Air Force Base, the second home of the B-1B and Barksdale, home of the vast majority of the 74 year old and still kicking B-52s, are not blurred.

It’s no surprise that Cape Canaveral Space Force Station (featured image), is parent base Patricks Space Force Base, and Vandenberg Space Force Base are all blurred. These locations are home to the bulk of military owned launch pads and house some of the world’s most advanced and secretive satellites ever built.

But no need to worry too much, for now it seems that Kennedy Space Center and its historic launch pads, LC-39A and LC-39B, is not blurred. That doesn’t mean NASA isn’t on the list, Wallops Flight Facility, a primarily civil research focused air field owned by NASA is blurred, but it’s launch pads, also owned by NASA, are not.

Finally, two other locations that may be top on the list of online map explorers, Groom Lake (Area 51) and the Los Alamos National Laboratory and also now blurred.

Without a formal announcement from Apple, we aren’t sure how quickly the company plans to blur over future bases; and if it’s just highly sensitive facilities or if all government locations are on the list to be blurred.

Some questions that I now have are how navigation works on these blurred bases. Does Apple CarPlay work still? Or if military personnel and civilians working at these bases need to find a new service for on base navigation needs.

#3354. Journey Now Say Their Farewell Tour Isn’t the End. What Could That Mean?

On Nov. 28, Journey will bring their “Final Frontier” farewell tour to a close with a homecoming show at San Francisco’s Chase Center. “It just feels like a good time to get off the train,” keyboardist Jonathan Cain said shortly before the tour began. “You’ve got to at some point say enough’s enough. It’s a grind, man. I just feel like this tour is a beautiful closing chapter…It’s time to move on.”

The first indication that the goodbye in San Francisco wouldn’t truly be a farewell came in September, when their name appeared on the 2027 Stagecoach festival lineup. But this was a makeup date, since their planned Stagecoach performance this year was rained out. It seemed like Stagecoach was possibly going to be a quickie encore show that truly marked the end of the band.

But earlier this week, Journey founder Neal Schon shared a message on Facebook that made it very clear their future plans involved a lot more than Stagecoach. “After completing 110 shows in 2026, we’ve felt something powerful happen within Journey,” he wrote. “Playing two and a half hours each night in our ‘Evening with Journey’ shows—the longest shows we’ve ever played—has brought us closer together, both musically and personally. Our fans have touched our hearts and helped pull us together. Your love, energy and passion for this music have reminded us how much we still share and how much this journey means to all of us. What began as ‘The Final Frontier’ now feels more like ‘The Long Goodbye.’ We’re letting our hearts—and the connection we feel with you every night—help guide what comes next.”

And despite numerous unambiguous statements that he was stepping aside after this tour, Cain is also seemingly changing his mind. “I’m overwhelmed with the turnout on this tour,” he recently told Ultimate Classic Rock. “It’s so strong. The fans have just been terrific. I’ve always looked at it like, well, you’ve got to know when it’s time to walk away, but just judging from this turnout, maybe we think about it. Right now we’re focusing on this tour. We’ve played everywhere we can play, and we’ve really been beating the bushes. I think it’s time for a little bit of a rest, so we’re gonna leave it here and see what happens.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Journey have been through more unpredictable twists and turns than just about any other rock group in history. It’s difficult to know exactly what’s going to happen in the future, but here are seven possible scenarios — and one that isn’t happening no matter how desperately some of you might wish to see it.

The simple and obvious move is to shrug off the whole “farewell tour” thing and just keep touring with this exact lineup. That would be the move from the playbook of the Who, Kiss, Mötley Crüe, Ozzy Osbourne, Tina Turner, Slayer, and just about every other act in music history that staged farewell tours. Some of these artists genuinely intended to step aside before changing their minds years later, and others simply saw a reliable gimmick to dramatically increase ticket sales and had no actual intention of retiring. In either case, there’s no rock & roll police force to stop groups from booking additional tours after their farewell runs end. Some jilted fans might stay home in the future, but the vast majority will come back.

One day before Journey kicked off their supposed farewell tour, Journey frontman Arnel Pineda told Rolling Stone that he nearly left the band prior to this tour. “Back in 2024, I said to them, ‘If you’re planning to do a farewell tour, you better tell me, because my issues and my personal problems are getting more intense, and I don’t know if I want to go with you,'” he said. “I said, ‘I want you to discuss the schedule with me.’ It is what it is now…. But then, I was really not happy with how they scheduled this tour. My body has changed. I can’t take the cold weather anymore.” Related Content Journey Drummer Deen Castronovo Suffers Medical Emergency During Tulsa Concert Journey Brought Out Hugo Valenti for a Second Time — And This Time He Nailed It Watch Longtime Steve Perry Impersonator Hugo Valenti Finally Guest With Journey Journey Add 40 Additional 2026 Dates to Final Frontier Farewell Tour

Schon confirmed his account. “It’s been very confusing,” he said. “He sent a lot of messages that he was overwhelmed with his personal life and didn’t know if he could do it. But we all signed contracts…Whatever goes down, I’m ready to plow through it, survive, and float to the top…I love Arnel. He’s been a total martyr, like a warrior.”

After the final bow in San Francisco, Pineda will likely have fulfilled the terms of his contract with concert promoters AEG. It’s certainly possible he feels better about sticking around and will sign on for additional tours. But it’s also possible he’s planning on heading back to the Philippines, never to return. In that case, they’ll need yet another new lead singer.

Back in 1998, singer Hugo Valenti — who bears a striking physical and vocal resemblance to Steve Perry — got a call from Sony A&R rep John Kalodner about possibly joining the band. But the idea was nixed before he could even audition. “I remember seeing him in a video, and he looked exactly like Perry, which I thought was really weird,” Schon said in 2003. “I said if we are going to get somebody with him looking exactly like Perry, I thought that was a little too weird!” Valenti went on to front the successful Journey tribute band Voyage, and now leads an entity called Hugo – The Ultimate Journey Tribute.

But in August, out of nowhere, Journey invited him onto their stage at two shows on their Japanese tour, where he sang “Faithfully” and “Keep on Runnin’.” He had some vocal problems on night one due to issues with his in-ear monitors, but sounded much better at the second show. Might this have been a test run for a future incarnation of Journey? (This may sound unlikely, but Robbie Krieger and Ray Manzarek initially rejected longtime Jim Morrison impersonator Dave Brock when they formed a new version of the Doors in 2002, but eventually made him a part of the band.)

Several lead singers have fronted Journey over the years, including Gregg Rolie, Robert Fleischman, Steve Perry, Steve Augeri, and Jeff Scott Soto. They reached the zenith of their popularity with Perry, and continuing without him initially seemed like a ludicrous proposition. But once they hired Arnel Pineda in 2007, the group was once again headlining arenas and even the occasional stadium. There’s no reason they can’t find another young, hungry singer to take Pineda’s place should this become necessary. (Valenti is 65 and perhaps not quite ready for the intense rigors of a long Journey tour.) They found Pineda on YouTube, and there must be at least one person on this planet capable of filling his shoes. They just have to start looking.

Prior to Steve Perry joining the band in 1977, original Santana lead singer Gregg Rolie provided the lead vocals from behind a keyboard. And on this tour, Pineda steps to the side quite a few times to grab a breath and allow Cain, drummer Deen Castronovo, and keyboardist Jason Derlatka a chance to sing a song or two. They all do remarkable jobs, especially Castronovo. It’s slightly hard to imagine, and it might take them out of arenas and into smaller venues, but they could continue to play Journey shows with Cain, Castronovo, and Derlatka handling all the vocals.

Back in 2019, when Journey were on a brief break, Schon hit the club circuit with a new group he called Journey Through Time. It included Rolie and Castronovo, and the shows dug deep into the Journey catalog and resurrected songs they hadn’t touched in decades. This thrilled hardcore Journey fans, but enraged the other members of the group. They felt the name was simply too close to Journey. That’s why Journey Through Time lasted for just a matter of days.

But Schon recently trademarked the name Journey Beyond, and he’s hinted that’s the name of his next project. If Journey indeed decides to call it a day, Cain actually retires, and Schon doesn’t face another legal hurdle over the name, it’s quite possible the future of Journey is Journey Beyond. It’s unclear who would be in such a group, but OG fans would love to see Rolie back. It would bring the saga full circle.

This one feels the least likely, but it is worth considering the possibility that Journey have a change of heart about their change of heart and never play again in any form after Stagecoach. But who are we kidding? That’s not going to happen. It’s more likely they’ll tour until Neal Schon is too old and feeble to hold a guitar, and then they’ll likely take a page from the Foreigner playbook and just license the name out to a bunch of randos. As long as people are willing to go out and see “Journey” play the hits, there will likely be some version of the group happy to take their money. We live in a world of vast possibilities. The fact that any of us even exist is the product of wildly unlikely circumstances, and yet here we all are. If you believe in the multiverse theory popularized by comic books and Rick and Morty, there are infinite versions of reality where anything that’s possible is actually happening. That includes worlds where hammerhead sharks have wings and fly, black olives are currency, and William “Refrigerator” Perry served six terms as president after single-handedly fighting off an alien invasion. But in none of these infinite worlds does Steve Perry return for a Journey reunion tour. A certain contingent of fans will never let the dream go, but it’s never, ever, ever happening. Everyone needs to accept this and move on with their lives.

#3353. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3352. How AI Will Change Chip Design

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

Confirm the kits have moved on and restore the patch

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After an unusually warm fall, many yards are still showing signs of late-season wildlife activity. Extended mild weather encourages wild rabbits to breed later into the year than usual, meaning shallow nests that typically appear in mid-spring can linger well into the cooler months.

As you head out for late-season garden tidy-ups, raking leaves or giving the grass a final cut can easily unearth a suspicious depression in the turf.

Before running the mower across it or filling it in, a quick check ensures the young have safely vacated the nest and that your lawn can be tidied without disturbing any remaining kits.

Most people picture rabbits living in deep underground tunnels, but garden rabbits actually raise their babies right on the surface. Instead of digging down, a mother rabbit scrapes out a shallow, bowl-shaped dip in the grass, tucked under a bush, or even sitting out in the open lawn.

To hide the spot from predators, she covers the hollow with a blanket of dried grass, dead leaves, and plucked fur. Because the nest sits completely level with the rest of the lawn, it looks just like an ordinary patch of dead grass until you step closer and notice the woven fur and bedding on top.

Now that temperatures have dropped and we're into the colder stretch of fall, any late-season litters should have already moved on.

If the grass cover has caved in, feels cold to the touch, is blowing apart in the wind, and shows no signs of wriggling underneath, the nest has been abandoned.

If you want to be completely sure before touching it, place two small twigs in an "X" over the top and leave them overnight. If the twigs are still sitting in the exact same spot the next morning, you can safely assume the nest is empty.

Once you know the nest is empty, clearing it away takes just a couple of minutes and stops pests from taking up residence in the leftover bedding. Slip on a pair of garden gloves and lift the clump of fur, leaves, and dried grass out of the dip.

If you are worried about lingering fleas or mites, use a garden trowel to scoop out the top layer of underlying soil along with the bedding. Seal the material in a bag and toss it straight into your garden waste bin.

Finally, level out the dip by filling it with a simple mix of topsoil and sand. Press it down firmly with your foot so it sits flush with the rest of the grass, then scatter a handful of lawn seed over the top so the bare patch fills back in before winter.

#3349. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#3347. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR looks awesome, but I’m not rushing to upgrade

After five years, Apple released its first major MacBook Pro overhaul since the M1 Pro/M1 Max models, and well… it was a little bit underwhelming from a design perspective. The product is incredible on many merits, but after seeing it, I’m not left feeling like I need to buy one – at least not yet.

The new MacBook Pro is substantially lighter. That’s a major improvement, especially if you’re someone who carries around a 16-inch MacBook Pro. With this new PROLED XDR generation, the 14-inch model reduced in weight by 0.5 pounds, and the 16-inch model reduced by 0.7 pounds. That’s a great deal when you’re carrying it around in a backpack or similar. The new models are also marginally thinner.

For me, though, I find myself a bit surprised by the fact that nothing about the top case design changed. The keyboard, trackpad, speaker, and port layouts all look about the same, and the chassis didn’t change shape besides getting a bit thinner. For every MacBook Pro overhaul in the past, the top case has changed in a meaningful way. With this overhaul, it really feels like more of a display upgrade that’s also accompanied by a lighter chassis.

Was there anything wrong with the current MacBook Pro chassis? Not at all. However, you could also argue the same for most design shifts in Apple’s history. It would’ve been nice to have a slightly different look, beyond the display.

This is more of a personal point. That said, I already have an M4 Pro model, and given the fact that these new MacBook Pros are substantially more expensive ($400 more compared to the miniLED MacBook Pros, which are also $300 more than they were prior to the June price hikes), I’m not particularly excited to buy silicon that isn’t the latest and greatest. The M5 family kicked off last year, and we already know M7 is coming next year.

I fully understand why Apple opted to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but it sure does make this MacBook Pro feel ever so slightly more uninteresting.

Apple already alluded to the fact that they have more in the pipeline when it comes to macOS optimizations for touch, so maybe I’ll be wowed in the future. For now though, aside from being able to interact with the iOS simulator with proper touch, I don’t really see much of a need to have touch on my Mac.

It’s great that it’s there, and I’m certainly not disappointed that Apple added it – but I’m not yet convinced I truly need it.

None of this was to bash on the new MacBook Pro at all. In fact, I’ll most definitely be buying one in the future, most likely once it gains M7 Pro and M7 Max chips by this time next year. Hopefully touch feels more important by then. I certainly love the idea of having a glowing Apple logo again, just not quite yet – and it’s not like this product will be going anywhere if I don’t buy it during the first iteration.

I bought a ridiculously overpowered M1 Max with 64GB of memory back when they were first released, and I have zero incentive to upgrade to this day. This machine covers all my needs with ease still.

It’s also worth noting I haven’t yet seen the new display in person. It’s totally possible I’ll be blown away once I see it, but I still think I’ll be capable of waiting. Especially since my M4 Pro MacBook Pro already has a 1000 nit display, so I’m not missing out too terribly from the OLED model.

How do you feel about the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR? Will you be buying one, or are you in a similar boat as I am? Let us know in the comments.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Get people to name Ridley Scott’s best movie and you’ll hear “Gladiator,” “Alien” or “Blade Runner,” but one of his finest in recent years is a film almost nobody saw in theaters. That movie is “The Last Duel,” a brutal, brilliant medieval drama from 2021 that flopped hard on release, but is getting its second wind on streaming thanks to platforms like Tubi.

Directed by Scott and based on Eric Jager’s book, “The Last Duel” dramatizes the true story of the last legally sanctioned duel to the death in medieval France. It tells the same events three times, “Rashomon”-style, from three different points of view, with the final version belonging to the woman at the center of it all. It pulled in just $30 million at the box office against a $100 million budget, but critics admired it, and in the years since it’s come to be regarded as one of Scott’s best films.

Now that it's streaming free on Tubi, there's no excuse not to give one of the most underrated movies of the decade the attention it always deserved.

J ean de Carrouges (Matt Damon) and Jacques Le Gris (Adam Driver) are close friends in 14th-century France, two men who once fought side by side in battle. But they couldn’t be more different. Carrouges is a proud, hot-tempered knight who feels the world owes him more than it’s given him, while Le Gris is charming, educated and quick to rise in the favor of their powerful lord, Count Pierre d’Alençon (Ben Affleck).

As Le Gris climbs and Carrouges keeps getting passed over for lands and titles he believes are rightfully his, their friendship devolves into a rivalry. Things escalate further when Carrouges marries Marguerite (Jodie Comer), a strong-willed noblewoman. While Carrouges is away, Le Gris forces his way into their home and assaults her.

When her husband returns, Marguerite does something extraordinarily dangerous for a woman of her time: She refuses to stay silent, naming Le Gris as her attacker. Enraged and determined to defend his wife’s honor, Carrouges petitions the king for a trial by combat, a duel to the death in which God is said to grant victory to whoever is telling the truth.

"The Last Duel" is an interesting mix of both rage and spectacle. I went in expecting a straightforward medieval epic, so I was surprised to realize it had a lot to say about truth and power dynamics — and, of course, believing women at its heart.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

As a "Rashomon" fan, the movie's three-perspective structure is what actually elevates it. Watching the exact same events replay from Jean’s self-serving point of view, then Jacques’s, then Marguerite’s, you start to notice how casually these men rewrite their own histories, and how differently a woman experiences the same moments the men barely register.

Matt Damon and Adam Driver are both excellent as the two rivals, Ben Affleck is a surprising addition I didn't see coming, and Jodie Comer is fantastic as Marguerite. And in the end, the final duel is one of the most viscerally intense sequences Scott has ever put to film.

If you're wondering about how it might leave you mentally when the credits roll, you can just sit with it at home to reckon with those feelings. Whatever the case, you should absolutely give it a watch, as you'll want to make sure you catch it while it's streaming free.

#3344. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

From ChatGPT to Gemini here's what you need to know about who sees your conversations

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You might tell ChatGPT things you’d never share with a stranger. Maybe you’ve asked it about a medical concern, argued with your spouse in a conversation about relationship advice or uploaded a document containing financial information.

But before your next conversation, here's something to know: Real people at AI companies may be able to read some of what you share.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic all have policies that allow certain conversations to be reviewed by humans, whether to improve their AI systems, investigate potential safety violations or troubleshoot problems.

That doesn’t mean someone is sitting behind a screen reading every message you send, but the assumption that your AI conversations are strictly between you and the chatbot is not accurate. Not to mention, just deleting a conversation doesn’t always mean the company deletes every copy immediately. In Google’s case, Gemini chats reviewed by humans can remain in company systems for up to three years, even after you delete your activity.

When you type a question into ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude, your message is typically sent to the company’s servers, where an AI model processes it and generates a response.

Most of that process is automated. But AI companies also use human reviewers to evaluate certain conversations. Several reasons might prompt a review; safety is a big one. AI companies use automated systems to detect potentially harmful requests, policy violations and suspicious activity. Some interactions may be escalated for human review.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Another reason conversations are reviewed is for improving the AI itself. Depending on your settings and the company’s policies, selected conversations may be used to evaluate responses, identify mistakes and help improve future models.

Companies generally describe measures intended to protect users during these reviews, including limiting access and removing identifying information. But removing a person’s name or account details doesn’t necessarily remove every sensitive fact contained in a conversation.

For example, a chat about a medical diagnosis, workplace dispute or financial problem could contain personal information even without the user’s name attached.

The important difference is that human review doesn’t happen to every conversation, and the rules vary depending on which chatbot you’re using.

OpenAI allows consumer ChatGPT conversations to be used to improve its models unless users opt out. You can disable this by opening Settings > Data Controls and turning off Improve the model for everyone.

But disabling training doesn’t mean every conversation becomes inaccessible to human reviewers.

OpenAI’s Data Controls FAQ explains that Temporary Chats aren’t used for training but may be reviewed to monitor abuse. Temporary Chats also don’t appear in your regular chat history and are generally deleted from OpenAI’s systems after 30 days.

For ordinary saved conversations, OpenAI says deleting a chat removes it from your account immediately and schedules it for permanent deletion within 30 days, unless the information has already been de-identified or must be retained for legal or security reasons.

Google is particularly explicit about how human reviewers may access conversations.

Google says conversations sent to service providers for review are disconnected from users’ accounts before being examined.

But there’s a significant catch: Chats reviewed by humans can be retained for up to three years, and deleting your Gemini Apps activity doesn’t remove those reviewed conversations.

Google also allows users to turn off its Keep Activity setting, which prevents future conversations from being used to train its AI models unless users submit feedback.

Even with that setting disabled, conversations may be retained for up to 72 hours to provide the service and for safety-related purposes. Google says some human review can still occur to help protect its systems and users. Essentially, disabling activity history reduces how your conversations are used, but it doesn’t guarantee that no human will ever see them.

Conversations suspected of violating Microsoft’s Code of Conduct may also be examined. Microsoft says users cannot completely opt out of human review because limited review is necessary when investigating suspected violations.

You can opt out of having future conversations used to train Microsoft’s generative AI models, but the company explains that this doesn’t prevent other uses, including security, compliance and certain product improvements.

That means switching off model training doesn’t provide a blanket guarantee against human access.

Anthropic also allows certain conversations to be reviewed, although it places restrictions on how that information is accessed. According to Anthropic’s explanation of who can view Claude conversations, conversations used for model improvement are separated from identifying account information before review.

Access is limited to a small number of personnel involved in model training, and Anthropic says it uses tools to filter or obscure sensitive information.

However, Anthropic also makes an exception for safety-related processing. Conversations flagged by its safety systems may still be used to detect harmful content, enforce policies and improve safety systems.

Claude’s Incognito Chats aren’t used for general model training and aren’t saved to chat history, but they’re still retained for a limited period, generally 30 days.

As with the other platforms, opting out of model training and preventing all possible review are two different things.

OpenAI generally schedules deleted ChatGPT conversations for permanent removal within 30 days, subject to exceptions for legal or security obligations and previously de-identified information.

Google’s policy is particularly worth clarifying because Gemini conversations that have been reviewed by humans can remain stored for up to three years, even after the user deletes their Gemini Apps activity.

This doesn’t mean every deleted conversation is kept for three years. The policy applies to conversations that have undergone human review. But it does highlight why users shouldn’t assume deleting a chat is equivalent to immediately erasing every copy of the information.

It’s also worth remembering that turning off model training usually affects how conversations are used, not necessarily how long they’re stored or whether they can be accessed for safety reasons.

Products such as ChatGPT Enterprise and business-focused AI services often provide additional contractual protections, administrative controls and restrictions on the use of customer data for model training.

But those protections vary by provider and product. They shouldn’t be mistaken for a universal guarantee that no authorized person can ever access customer information.

For everyday users, the safest assumption is that paying for an AI chatbot primarily provides access to additional features and capabilities, not the same confidentiality protections you’d expect from a doctor, lawyer or other professional relationship.

The good news is that all four major platforms provide controls that can reduce how your conversations are used.

These settings can make a meaningful difference, but none should be interpreted as a promise that conversations can never be reviewed for safety, security or legal reasons.

If you’re using AI regularly, a few precautions can significantly reduce the amount of personal information you expose.

2. Remove identifying details before submitting information. If you’re asking AI to analyze a document or help with a sensitive situation, consider replacing real names, addresses, account numbers and other identifying details with placeholders. Be mindful that context can sometimes reveal someone’s identity even after obvious identifiers have been removed.

4. Use temporary or incognito conversations when appropriate. ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude offer options designed to limit saved history and model training. These modes don’t necessarily prevent short-term retention or safety-related review, but they can reduce unnecessary exposure.

5. Consider running AI locally for particularly sensitive work. Tools such as Ollama and LM Studio can run supported AI models directly on your computer. When properly configured to process information locally without sending it to external services, they can reduce the need to upload sensitive information to a cloud provider. Just remember that local AI applications may still have optional online features or network connections.

The companies behind ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot have different policies, but they share one important reality: Some conversations may be accessible to human reviewers under certain circumstances.
