#3341. Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

His data systems make sure Claude’s answers are accurate

IEEE Senior Member Gurmeet Saran is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind Claude’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone.

Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San FranciscoTitle Member of technical staffMember grade IEEE senior memberAlma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement, the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models, Saran says.

“We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.”

Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab.

“I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity.

After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani. In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani.

While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions.

“We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.”

The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more.

With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic.

From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits, an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products.

Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies.

“IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.”

Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos.

“This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site.

That system, Metric360, eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics.

He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront, a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure.

Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff.

To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins.

“It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.”

His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve.

“AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.”

Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says.

“I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.”

“After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.”

He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work.

“We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.”

Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3340. What’s a ‘Winyah’? Fans of This Edgy Indie-Rock Band Can Tell You

What on earth is a Winyah? For many, it’s a bay in South Carolina. But for a growing audience of indie-rock fans, it’s the name of their new favorite band.

Named after that very body of water — Winyah Bay — in their home state, the five-piece mixes hard-driving Southern rock with youthful folk stylings to join a rock-edged new wave of bands like Dexter and the Moonrocks, Fox N’ Vead, and Cigarettes at Sunset. Winyah first became an entity in 2023 and played Bonnaroo in 2024, before dropping their debut album, Lot to Learn, the following year. That gave rise to a tour that featured a Lollapalooza showcase and back-to-back sellouts at New York’s Bowery Ballroom. Now, Winyah’s challenge is to harness that momentum with their sophomore LP, Right Here, Right Now, which dropped in mid-September.

Right Here, Right Now is their second LP on Evan Honer’s Cloverdale Records label and features 11 tracks, nearly all of which were written on bass player Stephen Russell’s back porch in September 2025, when the group caught a break between tour dates.

“It’s the first body of work that we ever wrote all together,” frontman Thomas Rowland says. “We came out of it with some songs that we really liked, but it was crazy. You really do have your whole life to write the first album and then such a short time to write the second one. It was a learning experience. It was us figuring out how to write together, and we’re still learning.”

Winyah is Rowland, Russell, keyboardist Robert Buffington Jr., guitarist Luke Gordon, and drummer Jake Riley. They took root playing bars in beach and college towns across South Carolina, and, quite quickly, realized they were on to something. They wrote the songs that make up Lot to Learn to give themselves enough original material to fill a set and, 25 million streams later, are figuring out the rest on the fly.

“Soundchecks, a little bit,” Gordon says of how the band shapes its musical identity. “As time grew between writing the first album and the second album, we all started collectively really enjoying each other’s influences and getting into them a lot more than we were before. It blossomed into a song here and a song there, and it came together.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Lyrically, Right Here, Right Now feels grounded in the band’s collective lives. “Lust” and “8 Missed Calls” both lament either romance or situationships, with the latter featuring the line, “I hate texts, their permanence/care too much, plays like disrespect/overthink and never respond.” Meanwhile, crash cymbals and electric guitar keep Rowland’s Carolina drawl from drifting too far into a folk sound. When he’s not fronting Winyah, Rowland lives in Nashville and works as a songwriter, collaborating with artists like Liam St. John, Brendan Walter, and Leon Majcen.

But Winyah burst onto the scene as a predominantly rock band, and that’s how they plan to stay. A Winyah show is not a rowdy, beer-slinging concert like some of the groups to whom they’ll inevitably draw comparisons as it’s a spectacle of swaying fans and raised smartphones. At their Bowery Ballroom shows — the New York city gigs in May of this year that became the group’s benchmarks — Gordon crowd-surfed from the stage to the middle of the room and back, playing guitar the whole time.

Winyah has already opened for Honer, Mt. Joy, and Wilderado, picking and choosing elements of each act to help shape their own sets. In October, they toured Europe for the first time and will return to New York in November to play the 1,800-capacity Brooklyn Steel, more than twice the capacity of Bowery Ballroom. That show is already sold-out. Trending Stories Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Andy Garcia, David Foster, Paul Anka Lead Kennedy Center Honors Yes, Matt Damon and David Letterman Were Background Actors on ‘The Gilded Age’ Season Premiere Britney Spears Says Kevin Federline and Jamie Lynn Spears Made Her ‘Feel Like a Slave’

“We started very much as a live band,” Russell says. “When you talk around, you learn that’s not how everyone starts, but it felt so obvious and natural to us. That’s what being a band was — playing live shows before we even had music.”

#3339. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Pumpkin Lights’ adds a fun jack-o-lantern to your Mac’s menu bar

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Pumpkin Lights is a nifty little menu bar app for Mac that lets you quickly toggle between light mode and dark mode with a ray-traced jack-o-lantern that drops down from the top of your screen. It’s completely free, and very fun to utilize.

If you remember the Festivas menu bar app from Mac year, Pumpkin Lights is very similar in concept.

Pumpkin Lights brings a jack-o-lantern to your menu bar, just in time for halloween. It’s a nice decoration, and there’s plenty of different ways to customize it. You can “grow” many different pumpkin designs, as well as pick between four different color variants.

When you click on the pumpkin or pull on it, your Mac will toggle between light and dark mode – at least by default. Pumpkin Lights also has the option to open an app/website, keep your Mac awake, mute a sound, run a command, or run a shortcut of your choice.

The jack-o-lantern does have proper physics, so you can actually toss it around a bit and move it around in a novel way. You can customize the rope it hangs from, and much more. There’s also an option to have a hanging light bulb that serves a similar purpose.

Why Pumpkin Lights? Here’s what the developer has to say:

The idea came from something most of us do every day without thinking: switching between Light and Dark Mode. It’s always a toggle buried in Control Center or System Settings, and it never feels like anything. I wanted it to feel like touching a real object. So instead of a flat icon, the pumpkin and the bulb are real 3D models, ray-traced in real time, hanging on cords you can swing and spin. When the candle lights, its glow comes through the carved face. I spent most of my time on small details like how the cords move and how light falls on the pumpkin, because I wanted it to still feel delightful the hundredth time you use it, not just the first.

Pumpkin Lights is a completely free utility. You can download it from the developer’s website here, and it’s available for any Mac running macOS 14 Sonoma or later. You can also follow the developer on Twitter.

#3337. IEEE Continues Preparations for the Realignment of Its Regions

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The redrawn IEEE region map that will become effective in 2028.

Progress continues in restructuring IEEE’s geographic regions, as outlined in The Institute’s February 2023 article “IEEE Is Realigning Its Geographic Regions.”

The restructuring is defined in the image of the redrawn map in this article.

Although the new regional alignment will not officially take place until 1 January 2028, several activities have begun within IEEE Member and Geographic Activities (MGA) and across other IEEE organizational units. Within MGA, volunteers and staff have been actively addressing system enhancements, director/director-elect elections, governance updates, communications, and regional finances and offerings.

Work will continue from now until the effective date of realignment in 2028. The change will not affect your IEEE membership, nor will it change either your local IEEE section or chapter.

If you have any questions regarding the realignment, contact Reg-Realignment@ieee.org.

IEEE Member and Geographic Activities oversees IEEE membership and the activities of its geographic units worldwide.

#3336. Wednesday and Mannequin Pussy Storm Nashville on the Rolling Stone Rock Tour

The members of Mannequin Pussy and Wednesday come together backstage for a Bitch Cabal group shot.

The Rolling Stone Rock Tour has featured must-see performances from Geese, Bleachers, Die Spitz, Wet Leg, and MJ Lenderman over the past couple of years.

Truth Club, an indie band that shares a home state of North Carolina with Wednesday, opened the show.

Shortly before taking the stage, Mannequin Pussy’s Marisa Dabice, Kaleen Reading, Colins Regisford, and Maxine Steen take a moment for a group huddle.

Marisa Dabice formed Mannequin Pussy with her friend Athanasios Paul back in 2010. The lineup has changed a bit over the years, and Paul departed in 2021, but they’ve grown exponentially more popular with each passing year. Their 2024 LP I Got Heaven was a huge critical favorite, even if their band name has made it hard for them to land TV bookings outside of Everybody’s Live with John Mulaney.

Guitarist Maxine Steen joined the band in 2021, and was a key architect of I Got Heaven. She’s playing here alongside touring member Carolyn Hayne.

Colins “Bear” Regisford has been Mannequin Pussy’s bassist since 2016, and he steps up to the mic every single night to belt out the protest song “Pigs is Pigs.”

Dabice faced enormous pressure to change the band’s name once they started to gain a following, but she refused. “I think we all expected that the world would become less puritanical,” she told Rolling Stone in 2023, “but in fact the opposite is true.”

Mannequin Pussy and Wednesday draw largely young fans to their shows. “We’re often playing to people that are 15 and just discovering rock music for the first time,” Dabice said in 2023. “I don’t think the barometer for rock is what’s on the cover of Rolling Stone or the top of the Spotify charts. It’s at these types of shows, where people are experiencing a collective catharsis.”

After two years of grueling road work in support of I Got Heaven, Mannequin Pussy entered the studio earlier this year to cut their fifth album. Over the past few months, they’ve been sprinkling in new songs like “Material Gains.”

Karly Hartzman formed Wednesday a little under a decade ago, and eventually brought drummer Alan Miller, pedal steel player Xandy Chelmis, bassist Ethan Baechtold, and guitarist MJ Lenderman into the fold. Lenderman has been focusing on his solo career over the past two years, and guitarist Jake “Spyder” Pugh has taken his spot in the touring band.

Wednesday played nine songs from their 2025 LP Bleeds at the Truth, and added in a cover of “Lonely Girls” by Lucinda Williams.

Mannequin Pussy bassist Colins “Bear” Regisford watches Wednesday’s set from the side of the stage.

Members of Wednesday rock out during the show. “Karly Hartzman is the kind of writer who can whisk you right into a stranger’s life with just a few words,” Rolling Stone‘s Rob Sheffield wrote earlier this year. “Her songs add up to a rootsy portrait of small-town heartache, as she evokes her cast of losers and ­dreamers, exploring the loneliest ­cor­­ners of American life. It’s like encountering Eudora Welty if she learned her licks playing in Southern hardcore bands.”

Karly Hartzman broke up with longtime partner MJ Lenderman shortly before cutting Bleeds, but they finished the record together and remain on good terms. “I was really at a breaking point exhaustion-wise,” she told Rolling Stone in 2025. “But I think I’m definitely more proud of it than any other thing we’ve ever made.”

#3335. Here’s how the new MacBook Pro and macOS 27 are optimized for touch

Apple just unveiled the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, its first MacBook with a touch display. While Apple already added a handful of touch optimizations to macOS 27 Golden Gate earlier this year, there’s also a number of new optimizations that were unveiled alongside the new MacBook Pro. Here’s what Apple worked on.

With the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, the traffic light icons in the top left of an app window will get bigger when you’re tapping them, making the touch targets a little bit larger.

Gestures that you can normally perform on the trackpad can also be performed on the screen. Whether that be a three-finger swipe up for mission control, three-finger swipes to switch spaces, pinching to zoom, or scrolling on a web page. You can also access Spotlight from the Dynamic Island, similar to how iPhones handle it on iOS 27.

If you’re an app developer, you’ll really appreciate this change: with the new MacBook Pro, you can fully navigate the iOS simulator with touch. No need to try to replicate touch gestures on a trackpad.

When you interact with a context menu in the menu bar, each of the items within a menu will get a little bit larger for touch. Additionally, most optimized apps will have larger touch targets, even if the buttons don’t necessarily appear bigger.

All in all, there’s a handful of optimizations already in macOS 27 Golden Gate for the touchscreen MacBook Pro. On top of what was named here, Apple also added pull to refresh in Safari and slightly larger spacing between menu bar items to all Macs with macOS 27.

Yeeeeeeeah no. Interactions with any of the onscreen elements are incredibly tedious, sporadic, and glitchy. This isn’t the company Steve Jobs started, it’s just Microsoft with an Apple logo.

Apple also says there’s more to come on the Mac when it comes to touch optimizations, so we’ll likely see much more in store at the next WWDC.

What do you think about touch support on the new MacBook Pro? Are you looking forward to it eventually trickling down to every Mac? Let us know in the comments.

I've tested well over 50 coffee machines now. Manuals, bean-to-cups, superautomatics — even the lever Flair 49 Pro (yes, no electricity involved at all). But which is the ultimate best espresso machine... for beginners?

I would recommend something with a built-in grinder. While some people will tell you machines with built-in grinders are inherently inferior, I disagree. A "good" grinder can set you back hundreds of dollars — on top of your espresso machine. This can easily make your coffee setup almost a thousand dollars... and that's before the actual coffee beans.

So if you want your first espresso machine but you're not sure which one to get, let me help you out. I'd recommend the Breville Barista Express, which we awarded 4.5 stars in our review, and it remains a classic. And the best part? It's currently just $499 at Amazon — yes, the same price as the Breville Bambino Plus. So you're really getting that grinder for free.

The Barista Express remains one of the most popular and recommended espresso machines for a reason. Like every other Breville, it has a PID controller (although unadjustable, but better than no PID controller!), a powerful steam wand, and a built in grinder.

The Breville Barista Express is easy to use, making it ideal for newer home baristas. While you still need to dial in beans yourself, this is a skill all baristas should dedicate time to learning — and you'll notice your espresso tastes so much better once you've figured it out. Your espresso should pour like honey.

Like every other Breville, the Barista Express has a PID controller, which means the machine controls your water temperature at every stage of the brewing process. I would personally never buy an espresso machine without a PID controller (or similar). This ensures your espresso is never burned or weak, but just right.

You can also customize pre-infusion time: this is where you soak the grounds with water at low pressure, extracting nuanced and delicate flavors, before ramping up the pressure for a full extraction. But you also don't have to use this feature — you can just press the "shot" button and espresso will come out.

So while the Breville Barista Express has a range of enthusiast features like adjustable pre-infusion and a PID controller, it also has a built-in grinder and easy-to-use steam wand. This machine will grow with you, from your early days of Googling things like: "What is espresso???" all the way to your serious barista era.

It's the Goldilocks of coffee, so to speak. And because the Bambino Plus is $499 full price, you're kind of getting the built-in Baratza grinder for free.

#3333. Amazon Prime Members Can Get Two Free E-Books in November

You can get thousands of free e-books over the course of 2026 if you know where—and when—to look. All year long, Amazon is offering free Kindle e-books to readers, with new opportunities popping up every month. In November, Prime members can get two free Kindle e-books from Amazon's First Reads program.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). This will send the e-book directly to the Kindle linked to your Amazon account. You can see what it should look like from the screenshot below.

You’ll know you did it right when you see a “Thanks, [your name]!” order summary indicating the e-book is being auto-delivered to the Kindle Cloud Reader.

This month, you can choose one from nine new Kindle e-books, plus this month's short read. Amazon notes the genre for each of the books above the title, offering a quick way to narrow down your options. (If you hover over the "See Editor Notes" under the "Shop Now" button, you'll be able to read a short description from the First Reads editor who picked the book.)

#3331. Can Dems Actually Win the Senate? Here’s a State-by-State Guide

The midterm elections are finally here, and all signs point to a successful showing from Democrats. The party has long been expected to take back control of the House of Representatives, but the Senate seemed like a pipe dream … that was until Donald Trump launched a war against Iran, driving costs up and causing his popularity to crater. Republican candidates have suffered as a result, and the GOP is suddenly in danger of losing Senate seats in red states they’ve held safely for years.

“Democrats are recognizing this opportunity and hoping that party leaders and the candidates that are able to finish the deal and win in these places where they have been extremely weak for decades,” Tatishe Nteta, provost of political science at UMass-Amherst, recently told Rolling Stone, noting that their polling has found “a clear enthusiasm gap between Democrats and Republicans about voting in the midterm election.”

“[Winning the Senate would] do untold damage to the Trump agenda for his last two years in office,” Nteta adds.

So how would Democrats have to perform on Tuesday to actually win the Senate, take total control of Congress, and put Trump and his administration on the defensive for the remainder of the president’s term?

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. Vice President JD Vance represents a tie-breaking vote in an evenly split Senate, which means Democrats need to pick up a net of four seats to lock down the majority. There are 35 Senate seats up for election this year, 13 of which are particularly competitive. Nine of these seats are currently controlled by Republicans, which means whichever party wins the majority (seven or more) of these 13 seats will likely win control of the Senate. Democrats are in pretty good shape — according to the latest polls, anyway — including in red states like Texas and Ohio, but it’s going to be very, very close.

Current status: Republican Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Who’s running: Texas’ MAGA Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic State Rep. James Talarico. Paxton defeated current Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary earlier this year.

Election Day: Polls close as early as 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Texas may be the grand prize of the 2026 midterms. A Democrat has not won a statewide election in the Lone Star State in over three decades, but this year conditions might be just right for the party to achieve the elusive Texas flip. Trump’s popularity is so low that it’s dragging down the Republicans who are actually on the ballot, including Paxton. At the same time, the Texas constituencies that Trump managed to bring onboard in 2024 are being pummeled by his economic and immigration policies. To top it all off, Paxton is a notably weak candidate, with an extensive history of public corruption and little experience running a competitive campaign. While Republicans have settled on trying to paint Talarico as a “woke” warrior obsessed with trans kids and socialism, the former seminarian has run a highly disciplined campaign focused on economic issues, anti-corruption, and a common sense “love thy neighbor” ethos. He’s got a good shot but — like trying to kick the football Lucy is holding — Texas Democrats have ended up on their ass too many times to count, and the state won’t be a guarantee until it’s been won.

What are the polls saying: Polling shows a narrow race between Paxton and Talarico, with the Democrat consistently leading by a single-digit margin in most major polls. Trump and Republicans are pouring stupid amounts of money and time into the state to try to drag Paxton over the line, and gin up turnout. Whatever the outcome, it’s looking like it will be a nail-biter on election night.  Related Content Bruce Springsteen Backs Abdul El-Sayed for Senate: ‘A Fighter Against the Corrupt’ Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Drop My Chemical Romance Lawsuit, but War of Words Rages On Trump Uses Final Pre-Midterm Speech to Ramble About Reflecting Pool Timbaland Sues Ex-Managers for $15 Million, Fires Back at Claim He Blew Fortune

Who’s running: Epidemiologist and local public health official Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, and former Republican House Rep. Mike Rodgers. Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is retiring at the end of his term.

Election Day: Polls close as early as 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: This one’s been pretty ugly. Michigan, a state with a large Muslim population, has become the nexus of Democrats’ internal war over how the party — and the United States — should respond to the ongoing genocide in Gaza. Rogers sailed through the GOP primary, while the progressive El-Sayed fought a tooth-and-nail campaign against moderate Hayley Sevens — a pro-Israel Democrat backed by Senate leadership and tens of millions in outsider spending.

El-Sayed — an economic populist and advocate for universal healthcare — managed to pull off the win for the nomination over Stevens, who has since endorsed his candidacy, but the race has remained a mess of ideological and culture war proxy battles. Rogers and Republicans have attempted to malign El-Sayed’s Muslim faith by promoting false links to extremism and terrorist movements. They’re also doing all they can to highlight his association with socialist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. All in all, both Republicans and Democrats are framing El-Sayed’s candidacy as symbolic of the progressive left’s ambitions toward higher office.

The race became even more chaotic days before the election, when Stevens endorsed Rogers after feeling jilted by the El-Sayed campaign. Will it matter?

What are the polls saying: That it’s too close for anyone’s comfort. El-Sayed has led in most major polls. Recent polling shows he may be building a lead as the campaign season enters its terminal phase, with a late September Maris poll giving him a seven-point advantage, and the final New York Times/Siena poll putting him up 11.

Who’s running: Republican incumbent Jon Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown

Election Day: Polls close at 7:30 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Ohio is bit of a strange case: Longtime Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who was ousted by Republican Bernie Moreno in the 2024 election, is looking to win back a seat in the Senate by knocking off incumbent Jon Husted in a special election to fill the seat vacated when J.D. Vance became vice president. Husted, a former lieutenant governor, was appointed to the seat by Gov. Mike DeWine in 2025, and hasn’t had long to establish himself as much of a political force. Brown has been a mainstay in the state for decades. Brown only narrowly lost his seat in 2024 with Trump at the top of the ticket — but now, with the president’s popularity in the dumpster, he has a good shot at winning back Ohio voters who see him as a safe, responsible, known quantity.

What are the polls saying: A Marist poll from late September has Brown up 51 to 43 over Husted. Ohio’s voters have overwhelmingly supported Trump each time he’s run, but the state’s strong ties to union labor and American industry mean that the brutal economic forecast has weakened their support for the overall Republican project. A recent Fox News poll showed that Ohio voters gave Trump a 42 percent approval rating, versus 57 percent disapproval. The final New York Times/Siena poll gave Brown a five-point edge.

Who’s running: Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper and former RNC Chair Michael Watley

Election Day: Polls close at 7:30 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: North Carolina is one of the most significant battlegrounds in the midterms, as retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis has decided to step down from his seat in a terrible climate for his party in the state. Roy Cooper, a Democrat and popular former governor of the state, has decided to step in — and thus far, he’s beating the pants off former RNC Chair Michael Watley. The gap is so big that the GOP’s top Super PAC has pulled ad funding from the state, figuring they’ll cut their losses and put the money into a more competitive race, like Kansas. Cooper is coming off two terms as the state’s governor, in which he presided over a popular and widespread Medicaid expansion.

What are the polls saying: The polls have Cooper up anywhere from +5 to +12. That could be overstating things, but considering Cooper was the first Democrat to beat a sitting Republican governor when he first ran in a statewide election in 2016 — with Trump on the ballot — it seems like about as safe of a bet as Democrats can get to flip a seat this cycle.

Who’s running: Longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, a former state senator

Election Day: Polls close at 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Woof. How long do you have? Democrats nominated Troy Jackson, an inoffensive, plainspoken former Maine state senator after getting off the absolute roller coaster of Graham Platner’s now-infamous candidacy. Platner’s journey from aw-shucks oyster farmer to poll-leading political juggernaut took the party by storm, and looked to put them in a commanding lead over Collins. That was until Platner’s past — which included a Nazi tattoo, repeated infidelity, and accusations of sexual assault — finally caught up with them. Jackson stepped in to fill the gap, and has been struggling to command the same kind of numbers while also navigating the delicate lane between straight talk and consultant-addled jargon. Collins, meanwhile, is currently weathering a shocking, blatant corruption scandal — although she’s proved almost impossible to unseat in the past, no matter the political headwinds.

What are the polls saying: It’s close. A New York Times poll from late September showed Collins up 49 to 46 over Jackson, but the same poll in early November has Jackson up five. An Emerson poll released just before the election had Collins up two.

Who’s running: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas is running against former Republican Sen. John Sununu. Current Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen is not seeking reelection.

Election Day: Polls close as early as 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: New Hampshire is a curious electoral case. In 2024, Vice President Kamala Harris barely managed to win the state. Its entire congressional delegation is Democratic, but the governorship and General Court (the fancy New Hampshire term for its state legislature) are Republican-controlled.

With name recognition, a monetary advantage, and persistent distaste among voters for Democrats, Sununu has managed to keep Democrats in the state on their toes, and may manage to squeeze out a much-needed victory for Republicans amid a potential blue wave election. Pappas on the other hand is riding the anti-incumbency wave beleaguering Republicans this cycle, and has flexed his credentials as a moderate Democrat to win over independents.

What are the polls saying: Recent polling has shown Pappas with a comfortable lead. The FiftyPlusOne polling average puts him at 51.8 percent to 43.0 for Sununu.

Who’s running: Incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff is facing off with Republican Rep. Mike Collins, a prominent Trump ally.

Election Day: Polls close at 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: In 2020, Ossoff helped deliver Democrats a 50-50 Senate majority under President Joe Biden. Now, in his first bid for reelection, Ossoff is reminding voters exactly how capable he is as a candidate, and even drawing speculation about a presidential run in 2028.

Collins, a close Trump ally and self-described “MAGA warrior” who supported Trump’s efforts to meddle with the GA election in 2020, is struggling to outrun his association with the president. Trump’s insistence that voters pretend he’s on the ballot seems to be dragging down the popularity of Republican candidates across the country, but Collins has continued to campaign alongside the president. Democrats will probably need to hold onto Ossoff’s seat in order to wrest the Senate majority from Republicans, and it seems like they have a good chance to do just that.

What are the polls saying: The race is rated as “likely Democratic” by the Cook Political Report, and Ossoff has built a solid lead in recent polls.

Who’s running: Democratic State Rep. Josh Turek is running against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson. Current Sen. Joni Ernst is not seeking reelection.

Election Day: Polls close at 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Iowa wasn’t really even on the map for Democrats until pretty recently. But in August, the Cook Political Report moved the race from a “lean Republican” to a “toss-up.” Turek, a professional wheelchair basketball player and Paralympic athlete, managed to make significant inroads in the state won by Trump three elections in a row. He was also the first 2026 midterm candidate to secure an endorsement from (and cut an ad with) former President Barack Obama, giving a massive boost to his national profile.

Describing himself as a “prairie populist,” Turek has focused his platform on a message of affordability, access to healthcare, and anti-corruption policies. He has hit Hinson, who is endorsed by Trump, over the growth of her personal wealth while serving in Congress. Hinson in turn has been forced to distance herself from the president on certain critical policy issues given Trump’s floundering approval ratings. All in all, if Democrats manage to pull off a flip in the heartland of Trump country, it will be its own special kind of victory.

What are the polls saying: That it’s pretty much a dead heat. Recent polls flip-flop between giving Turek and Hinson a roughly two-point lead, well within the margin of error.

Who’s running: Democrat Mary Peltola is challenging incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, who has two other Republicans to compete with, as well: Gerald Heikes and, confusingly, another Dan Sullivan.

Election Day: Polls close as early as 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Alaska’s election structure makes this a bit strange. For the second time, the state is using ranked choice voting to determine its senator. In some ways, it’s a traditional two-horse race: the Democrats have a viable challenger in Mary Peltola, and the Republicans have a longtime incumbent in Dan Sullivan who’s trying to hold his seat. But the RCV system makes things interesting in that there’s a second Dan Sullivan running, who has been accused of only entering in the race to siphon off votes from the incumbent Dan Sullivan. In the top-four election to decide the candidates, Peltola got over 49 percent of the vote, and Sullivan only got around 41 percent, with the other Dan Sullivan posting 2.5 percent and a couple other Republicans racking up a few percentage points here and there. Democrats think Peltola is their best shot to take a Senate seat in Alaska in years, but she’s not perfect. A recent New York Times report alleged that Peltola has a history of, in private, tossing slurs around and, shall we say, generally being an asshole to staff. It’s hardly a fatal scandal for her campaign, so we’ll have to see if it shifts the needle for voters in November.

What are the polls saying: Alaska is a conservative state in general, so most analysts have this one as a toss-up with a slight Republican lean — but still very much a battleground this fall. Pre-election polling has Peltola with a slight lead.

Who’s running: Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, is running to keep his seat, which she was appointed to after her brother’s death. Her opponent is Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician.

Election Day: Polls close at 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Also a strange one! Darline Graham is, as far as we can tell, barely campaigning. She’s a political novice who only seems half-interested in the job beyond backing Trump. But she’s got the full support of the GOP — sort of. The party brass is behind her, but after she won a contested primary, elements of the conservative movement are also trying to mount a write-in effort for Congressman Ralph Norman, who narrowly lost to Graham in the primary. (Norman, for his part, has said he’ll support Graham.) Andrews, meanwhile, is battling the massive recognition of the Graham name, but has closed the gap considerably and is posting predictable leads with younger demographics.

What are the polls saying: It’s extremely close. South Carolina is a red state through and through, but Graham’s weak candidacy has opened the door and pre-election polling has the race in a dead heat.

Who’s running: Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya, a former sports anchor. Current Sen. Tina Smith is not seeking reelection.

Election Day: Polls close at 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Minnesota is a true purple state where the Democratic Farmer Labor Party (DFL) has managed to dominate Democratic success through a focus on working-class, economically progressive governance. Tafoya is a bit of a known entity in her own right. Her career as an Emmy-winning journalist and sideline reporter for NBC’s Sunday Night Football is a leg up in terms of sheer name recognition. While a Republican hasn’t held one of Minnesota’s Senate seats since 2009, a massive benefits fraud scandal uncovered under Flanagan and Gov. Tim Walz’s administration has given Tafoya a competitive boost. Tafoya is leaning hard into the fallout of the state fraud scandal, accusing her opponent of turning a blind eye to the abuse as Minnesotans were cheated out of millions in government funds.

What are the polls saying: It’s close, but Flanagan seems to have the polling edge heading into Election Day.

Who’s running: Republican incumbent Roger Marshall is facing Democrat Adam Hamilton, a pastor.

Election Day: Polls close as early as 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Democrats think that they have an actual shot at Kansas for the first time in … 94 years. Hamilton is a relatively strong candidate: he’s a pastor who has made it explicitly clear that he does not want to be besmirched by the losing elements of the national party (“please, no,” he said when asked if he wanted Kamala Harris to come campaign with him). Kansas’ economy has been hit extremely hard by Trump’s trade policies and war in Iran, and Hamilton has even been endorsed by some Republicans, including one of Marshall’s primary opponents this year. Marshall, for his part, has been hit by a story alleging that he filed lawsuits against 700 of his patients when he was an OBGYN and has been struggling to paint the very normal, very moderate Hamilton as an “extremist.” The GOP has recognized this and is diverting resources away from their doomed effort in North Carolina to try to get Marshall across the finish line.

What are the polls saying: It was a dead head a month ago, but recent polls have shown Hamilton leading. Still, it’s been nearly a century since Democrats have won in the state.

Who’s running: Incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts is running against an independent candidate, Dan Osborn, who has inherited much of the Democratic Party’s support after Cindy Burbank, the Democratic primary winner, dropped out to make way for him.

Election Day: Polls close at 8 p.m. local time. Trending Stories Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback Andy Garcia, David Foster, Paul Anka Lead Kennedy Center Honors Yes, Matt Damon and David Letterman Were Background Actors on ‘The Gilded Age’ Season Premiere Britney Spears Says Kevin Federline and Jamie Lynn Spears Made Her ‘Feel Like a Slave’

How’s the race been shaping up: This is also a strange race, notably because it is far closer than expected but does NOT feature two candidates from the two major parties. Osborn is an independent, blue-collar, union member who came within single digits of beating Nebraska’s other senator, Deb Fischer, in the 2024 election. The race is close enough that Trump was forced to head to Nebraska for emergency rallies in early October, where he called Osborn a “fake independent who will say anything to get elected.” We’ll see if that’s enough!

What are the polls saying: This one is close but not as tight as some of the others on this list. Polls from late October show Ricketts has a narrow lead, and Nebraska’s heavy GOP bias still in place. Still, Osborn has a fighting shot at the seat.

RF and microwave systems increasingly depend on amplifiers and receivers that perform reliably across wide frequency ranges and demanding signal conditions. Confirming this performance calls for signal sources with wide output power range, low phase noise, and fast switching speed. Amplifier characterization relies on accurately measuring gain, compression, and intermodulation distortion, while receiver verification often involves simulating blockers, calibrating power accuracy, and substituting for local oscillator and clock circuitry during early design stages. This guide walks through these test applications step by step, showing how engineers and technicians can validate RF and microwave hardware across research, development, and manufacturing environments.

Its most recent outing, season 2, dropped on the streaming service on Oct. 21 and quickly shot to the No. 1 spot on the platform's top 10 charts.

But if you've already caught up with Pratt's James Reece and followed him through the last eight episodes of global espionage, sniper attacks and political coups and still want more, we've got three action-packed series to fill that void. (There's also, of course, "The Terminal List's" prequel series, "The Terminal List: Dark Wolf," which you should add to your watchlist if you haven't already.)

From a Golden Globe-winning British miniseries to a Taylor Sheridan-created spy thriller, here are three shows like "The Terminal List" to stream next.

Written and created by Jed Mercurio ("Line of Duty," "Bodies"), this six-part political thriller centers on Police Sergeant David Budd — played by Richard Madden, who earned a Golden Globe for Best Actor for the role — a PTSD-riddled war veteran who has been assigned as the principal security detail for the U.K. Home Secretary Julia Montague (Keeley Hawes), whose politics he loathes.

Budd soon finds himself caught not only in a web of conspiracy, corruption, and surveillance, but also in a conflict between his own loyalties. With Montague's past directly linked to the military conflict that left him physically and psychologically scarred, Budd must decide whether he wants to serve as the secretary's protector or instead be her greatest threat.

Along with neo-Western sagas, "Yellowstone" creator Taylor Sheridan also knows his way around high-octane thrillers and action-packed black-ops dramas. Loosely inspired by a real-life U.S. military support program called Team Lioness, this tense spy thriller follows CIA team leader Joe McNamara (played by Chris Pratt's "Guardians of the Galaxy" co-star Zoe Saldaña) as she goes undercover and infiltrates dangerous terrorist and cartel organizations by befriending the wives, daughters, and inner circles of high-value targets to take the criminal operations down from within.

#3328. This 140W power station might be the ultimate charger for Apple users [Video]

I have tested and used countless charging stations over the years, and while many of them get the job done, I feel like there is always some sort of compromise. Whether it’s not enough power, lack of a certain port that I need, or slow wireless charging, I have yet to find one that truly checks every box for me. But over the last month, I have been using CUKTECH’s new 140W Powerstation, and it has nailed everything. It is a six-in-one desktop charger with a built-in retractable cable, magnetic wireless charging, and a dedicated diagnostic display, all in an aesthetic, compact package. Here is everything you need to know and why I think it’s worth considering.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video to see this CUKTECH 15 PowerStation in action!

At its core, the CUKTECH 15 PowerStation is a 140W GaN charger. It can charge one device at the full 140W, meaning it can charge your 16-in MacBook Pro PROLED XDR at max speed, or it can divvy up that power to charge up to six devices at once. It also offers a great combination of ports, a built-in cable, and multiple wireless charging options. You get:

Of course, the biggest selling point is the versatility of it all. You can charge your MacBook Pro with the main USB-C port, charge your iPad with the built-in cable, place your iPhone on the MagSafe charger, and place your AirPods on the wireless charging pad. After all of that, there are still more ports for other accessories that I use daily.

Do keep in mind that the 140W output is the total output, so if more devices are added, that output is shared across all the connected devices.

I am someone who is constantly switching between so many Apple devices. I switch between my iPad Pro and MacBook Pro all the time, and now that it is techtember, I am testing multiple iPhones at the same time, so I need to make sure all of my devices are charged up for when I need them. Not only that, but I also need a USB-A port for my camera battery charging station. So having a centralized hub to charge all of my devices is a MUST in my desk setup. So what immediately stands out to me about the CUKTECH 15 is how much functionality they were able to pack into this relatively compact charging station.

I am a huge fan of built-in retractable cables; they eliminate the need to remember to carry a USB-C cable, so you know you can charge at least one device. Then you add in the wireless magnetic charging stand that supports the new iPhone Duo and StandBy Mode, all while keeping the iPhone upright and visible. Also, when you set up that magnetic charging pad in the upright position, it reveals an AirPods Pro charger. The design is so well thought out.

The cherry on top of it all is the display. I love being able to see how fast something is charging. It allows me to see whether products meet their charging speed standards and how different devices are affected by their charge levels. CUKTECH was also smart to still include one USB-A port. Lots of companies have decided to omit that port because it is an old standard, but there are still plenty of older and wacky tech that uses USB-A, so the inclusion is appreciated. The only thing missing is a dedicated Apple Watch charger, but I just plug in my own when I need it.

The CUKTECH 15 140W Charging Station is available today on Amazon for $149. It has been out in Europe for a little while, but now it has finally made it to the US!

There are plenty of charging stations on the market, but CUKTECH’s 140W power station is the first to check off all the boxes for me. It’s compact, looks great, has all the ports and charging methods I need, and features a beautiful TFT display that lets me know things are charging as they should. If you use multiple devices throughout the day and need them charged at all times, this is worth considering.

What do you think? Is this something you would use? How many devices do you normally have on you? Let’s discuss below!

#3326. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3325. Here’s how I’m solving the iPhone Duo kickstand problem, without any bulk

If you’re like me and bought an iPhone Duo, you’re likely a bit disappointed by the options on the market to prop it up on a table. Apple’s official $129 folio with kickstand is expensive, flimsy, and gets in the way of the outer display. MagSafe wallets that turn into kickstands are too tall for the back of the phone, and there aren’t many good third party cases yet.

That said, the perfect option for an iPhone Duo kickstand might’ve actually been hiding in plain sight all along.

The reason why I say it’s been hiding in plain sight is because this accessory isn’t actually designed for iPhone Duo, it works on all iPhones. It’s the PopSocket Low-Pro, a low profile MagSafe PopSocket with a ring that flips out and serves as a kickstand. It also works as a normal PopSocket if you’re interested in that.

This PopSocket has a few strengths on iPhone Duo:

On the last point, you might’ve heard from some iPhone Duo reviewers that the phone can’t really work on a MagSafe stand while unfolded, because the weight of the left half of the phone drags it down. I’m happy to report that this PopSocket actually largely fixes that. It’ll still slip slightly over a longer period of time, but it’s good enough to make the experience usable.

I tested this across multiple MagSafe stands of mine and the slippage issue is improved across the board when using the PopSocket Low-Pro.

My favorite advantage to the PopSocket Low-Pro is the fact that it improves the iPhone Duo experience greatly while still allowing you to rock the phone without a case. Given the fact that the iPhone Duo is already 11.3mm thick when it’s folded, I wasn’t jazzed about the idea of adding even more bulk to the phone.

The wireless charging speed and efficiency is expected to go down with more layers in between the magsafe magnets on the phone and the grip. With that said, sadly, this does worse than the Oh Snap grip/stand when it comes to wireless charging. The pop socket completely stops wirelessly charging if you have a case on, even Magsafe ones.

The Low-Pro is truly low profile, and can’t really be felt when you’re holding the phone. It protrudes a fair bit less than the camera bump does.

If you’re interested in purchasing a PopSocket Low-Pro, you can grab one on Amazon for $36-40 depending on the color option you’d like. Navy, Gun Metal, Black, Electric Fuschia, Teal, Carbon Lattice, Mint, and Tortoise are available for $40, while the Lilac and Orange colors are available for $36, a 10% discount.

The Asics Gel-Nimbus has been one of the most popular cushioned running shoes available for almost three decades, and as a result, Asics launches a new version of the sneaker each and every year.

This year’s version — the Asics Gel-Nimbus 29 — has just been announced, which means the time is ripe for savvy shoppers to start looking for deals on older models of the shoe.

I’ve been searching early Black Friday sales myself and found a $40 discount on the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28 on Amazon and REI, and a $65 saving on the Asics Gel-Nimbus 27 on Amazon, which brings it under $100.

All colors and sizes of the Gel-Nimbus 28 are reduced to $129 in the Amazon sale. It's a lighter shoe than the Gel-Nimbus 27 and a highly comfortable option for cruising through your daily training runs.

It's a couple of generations old now, but the Asics Gel-Nimbus 27 is still a reliable pick for runners seeking a comfortable, cushioned shoe. The price will vary based on size and color on Amazon, so click around to find the best deal for you.

Asics made updates to the Gel-Nimbus 29, but the changes to the upper and outsole are fairly minor.

A new engineered mesh upper aims to improve the fit, while great rubber coverage on the outsole should boost grip and durability, though these have not been problems with past models in my experience.

The midsole changes are more significant with the Gel-Nimbus 29 using a new foam called FF Luxe Plus, which is softer than the FF Blast Plus foam used in older versions of the shoe.

Asics has also reshaped the midsole a little to allow for more compression when you land, which should enhance the softer feel of the new midsole foam.

I’ve yet to get my feet into the new Nimbus to try out its new foam, which is also used in the Asics Slowcush, which is an even more cushioned option for daily running.

I have racked up a lot of miles in the Asics Gel-Nimbus 27 and Asics Gel-Nimbus 28, though, and both are reliable, durable options for your training runs.

Like the Gel-Nimbus 29, they are built for comfort on easy and long runs in particular, and do that job well. If you’re looking to round out a running shoe rotation with a highly-cushioned shoe for easy runs, they’re great options at much lower prices than the new shoe.

When picking between the 27 and 28, I’d be tempted to get the cheaper 27 myself. While the Gel-Nimbus 28 is lighter than the 27, it’s not really any better for faster runs, and at easy paces the lower weight wasn’t so noticeable for me.

However, the deals are more consistent on the Gel-Nimbus 28 — all sizes and colors are down to $129 on Amazon — whereas the price of the Gel-Nimbus 27 jumps around depending on the exact shoe you go for, so you might even get a better discount on the 28.

#3323. Band of Heathens’ Gordy Quist Shares Cancer Diagnosis

Gordy Quist, singer and guitarist of country quintet the Band of Heathens, announced that he has been diagnosed with Stage 3 colorectal cancer. In a post on the band’s social media, Quist told fans that the diagnosis came after a routine colonoscopy, and he had not been experiencing any symptoms.

“I would urge all of you to please get your colonoscopy if you are overdue,” Quist said in the video. “It’s super easy, not a big deal and I’m very fortunate that I went to get mine because I’ve had zero symptoms and likely would not have had symptoms for a while now.” He went on to share that he will not be touring with the band for the foreseeable future so he can “dive headfirst into this challenge” and focus on treatment — though he encouraged fans to still catch the Band of Heathens on tour with Donovan Frankenreiter and promised a collaborative show. (Quist co-founded the group with fellow vocalist Ed Jurdi in 2005.)

Quist ended the video by pointing to his personal site, where he will be posting updates on his health and treatment. In his first post, he reiterated the importance of regular colonoscopies. “If you’re 45 or older, or have ever had blood in your poop (regardless of your age), please go schedule your colonoscopy,” Quist wrote. “It’s really not a big deal. The prep is the worst part, and even that is mostly just a long evening getting very well acquainted with your bathroom. Most likely they’ll find nothing of concern. But if you’re in the unlikely position of having a tumor, time is of the essence.”

According to recent research, rates of colorectal cancer are rising in almost all age groups, including brackets too young to qualify for insurance coverage of a colonoscopy. After debuting the refreshed iPad mini with OLED this past week, Apple still has more in the pipeline for the rest of the iPad lineup in the first half of next year. That includes a new iPad Air, a new base iPad, and a new iPad Pro, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

#3321. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

The surprising truth behind your home's property value and data centers

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As AI drives demand for more computing power, the next wave of development is heading to America's neighborhoods.

According to an April 2026 Pew Research Center analysis, 67% of planned U.S. data centers are located in rural areas, compared with just 13% of facilities already operating. Perhaps more surprisingly, 39% of planned facilities are in counties that don't currently have a single data center. For some states, AI data centers are even on the ballot this Election Day as communities that have never had to consider the effects of a massive computing facility, now could soon face questions about electricity costs, water supplies, noise and property values.

A new analysis from Jones & Swanson brings several of these concerns together, examining how America's expanding data center footprint could affect the people living nearby.

And while the findings raise legitimate questions about the costs of AI infrastructure, they also challenge one common assumption: Living near a data center doesn't necessarily mean your home will lose value.

For homeowners, one of the biggest questions is whether a nearby data center will make their property less desirable.

The answer may be surprising. An August 2026 Realtor.com study examined 43 ZIP codes where large data centers opened between 2019 and 2025. Researchers compared those locations with similar neighborhoods that didn't receive a data center.

The analysis found no statistically significant difference in home price appreciation during the first two years after a facility opened. Oddly enough, homes near newly opened data centers generally gained value at roughly the same rate as comparable homes elsewhere.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Something to note, is that the study examined ZIP-code averages, rather than the experiences of individual properties. It also excluded Texas and 11 other states where transaction prices aren't publicly disclosed, and only tracked home prices for two years following a facility's opening.

There's another reason this matters. Realtor.com found that the median large data center opening in 2026 was located in an area with just 32 residential housing units per square mile, down from 116 in 2017.

As data centers move into less densely populated areas, their impact on individual communities could look different from what researchers have observed so far.

The biggest financial concern may be your electricity bill. Even if a nearby data center doesn't reduce your home's value, there's another potential cost homeowners should consider: electricity.

These facilities need enormous amounts of power to run servers and keep their equipment cool. And as more data centers connect to the grid, utilities may need to build additional power plants, transmission lines and substations.

The question is who ultimately pays for those upgrades. A June 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that data centers could account for 9.5% to 15.3% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, with a central estimate of 11.8%. That's a substantial share of national electricity demand for one category of infrastructure..

Virginia remains America's data center capital, with 674 facilities listed as operating, under construction, planned or land-banked, according to the Jones & Swanson analysis. Texas follows with 537, while California has 296 and Georgia has 276.

The Pew Research Center found that 87% of existing data centers are in urban areas. The pipeline of proposed facilities looks almost completely different, with two-thirds planned for rural locations.

The South and Midwest account for approximately three-quarters of planned facilities, with the South alone representing 48%.

But despite all the water, energy and land use, it's worth remember that not every data center is dedicated to AI. These facilities support everything from cloud storage and websites to streaming services and, yes AI.

If a data center is proposed near your home, there are several things worth investigating before local officials approve the project. Start with electricity costs. Ask your utility or local regulators whether new transmission lines, substations or generation capacity will be required and how those expenses will be allocated.

Water use is another important consideration. Developers should be able to explain where cooling water will come from, how much the facility expects to use and what happens if the community experiences a drought.

Residents can also ask about noise limits, backup generator testing, construction hours and whether landscaped buffers or other protections will separate the facility from nearby homes. Much of this information may be available through local zoning applications, planning board meetings, utility filings or environmental permit reviews.

It's also worth distinguishing between a project that has been proposed and one that has received all the necessary approvals. As the Pew research shows, a substantial portion of the country's future data center footprint remains in the planning stages.

America's AI boom is becoming a physical infrastructure boom, and its effects are reaching well beyond Silicon Valley and Northern Virginia. For homeowners, the latest research offers both reassurance and reasons to keep paying attention.

The evidence so far doesn't show that large data centers consistently reduce nearby home values, but questions about electricity costs, water demand, noise and infrastructure spending remain important, particularly as development moves into rural communities.
