#3301. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3300. No ‘Cliff Booth’ At Cinemark: CEO Cites Long-Term Industry Risk

Cinemark CEO Sean Gamble is calling the release model for The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth not great for the theatrical ecosystem, nor in the best interest of its theaters.

The no. 3 U.S. exhibitor — as well as no. 2 chain Regal — won’t be playing the Netflix film, Quentin Tarantino’s followup to Once Upon A Time In Hollywood, after the streamer set a two-week Imax theatrical window for the Nov. 25 release ahead of its Dec. 25 streaming debut. It will play at the biggest exhibitor AMC Theatres, and some indies in standard format as well.

“The Cliff Booth situation is an interesting one,” said Cinemark CEO Sean Gamble, asked about the release on a call after quarterly earnings. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'Blue Eye Samurai' Sets Season 2 Release Date At Netflix News Jason Statham & Guy Ritchie Reunite For Netflix Feature 'Dogfight'

“We book all of our films on a case-by-case situation. In that particular situation, we always look at things through a long-term lens and how certain precedents and things we might do could affect longer-term industry dynamics. In this particular case, we don’t believe the proposed release model is constructive for the broader theatrical ecosystem, and it’s not aligned with the greatest interest of our theaters.”

He also noted The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, “a huge movie that’s going to be opening immediately prior … from one of our major studio partners.

“The buzz on that film is pre-sales are through the roof. so our intention is to continue to play that in its second week as we will in its first week on our screens,” he said.

Regal also commented on the Cliff Booth window in a statement obtained by Deadline.

“Regal’s premium screens are among our most valuable assets, and one of the factors we consider in how we allocate them is the level of commitment distributors make to the theatrical marketplace,” said Brooks LeBoeuf, SVP of US Content, Regal Global Entertainment.

“Shortened theatrical windows have a direct impact on those decisions, as they limit the opportunity for audiences to experience films on the big screen. We will continue to prioritize releases that recognize the value of theatrical exclusivity, including The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which will have our full support in IMAX.”

Netflix has became more theatrical friendly, recently designating a handful of films for cinemas and formal box office reporting, although the windows vary. The first was a platform launch of festival favorite and awards contender La Bola Negra three weeks ago, followed by The Mosquito Bowl this past weekend. Greta Gerwig’s February release, Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew will have a 50-day window to streaming, and next holiday season’s Charlie Vs The Chocolate Factory a 47-day window.

“I think it’s probably early to kind of draw any conclusions,” Gamble said, “but they’ve certainly been taking more constructive steps towards engaging in a bigger way with theatrical. I mean, they’ve got six films announced now through November of 2027 that are going to be having full theatrical releases with marketing campaigns and communicated box office results. We’ll see how those get fully executed. So we’ve got to wait and see how that goes. But again, we see it as a positive step. And we continue to believe that, like all their peers, there’s substantial value for them … in a more meaningful theatrical presence.

“There’s obviously a lot of change happening at that company right now, so we’ll see where things go.”

He said streamers are at different stages of theatrical evolution.

“Amazon, clearly, is leaning most heavily into theatrical exhibition. Following their acquisition of MGM, they’ve stated multiple times their intention to ramp up to approximately 15 theatrical releases per year, and they’re close to that this year. So they definitely are in it in a big way. They put resources both domestically and internationally in place to make that happen from a distribution and marketing standpoint. So they’re clearly in it for the long haul, and we continue to see them moving in a positive direction.”

Apple, he noted, had great success with F1. “In the conversations that we’ve been having with Apple, we believe that they’re likely to start to ramp up a bit more before too long. What the scale of that is, I think, still remains to be seen. They haven’t made any firm commitments as of yet but at least we’re encouraged by what we’re hearing, of them stepping a bit more up into theatrical.”

#3299. Here’s everything new Apple TV has coming in November

Apple TV’s November lineup includes the return of a beloved comedy, a heist thriller with big stars, the follow-up film to its Oscar winner, and a lot more. Here’s everything new coming to Apple TV in November.

“Stick” is a sports comedy series created by Jason Keller and starring and executive produced by Owen Wilson. Wilson stars as Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill, ex-pro golfer whose career was derailed prematurely 20 years ago. After the collapse of his marriage and while working at an Indiana sporting goods store, Pryce hedges his bets, and future, entirely on a troubled 17-year-old golf phenom named Santi (Peter Dager). “Stick” is a heartfelt, feel-good comedy about a found family and their relationships set within the world of golf as it has never been shown before.

Hollywood actor and comedian Nora Lum (aka Awkwafina) is the descendant of restaurant royalty … but she can’t cook. Join the star on an inspiring culinary road trip as she learns the craft and attempts to revive her family’s beloved Chinese eatery.

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

They wouldn’t take Judy Heumann’s phone calls, so she took their building. In 1977, a young disabled woman (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Siân Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

In the latest special under the acclaimed “Snoopy Presents” banner, the Peanuts kids are on their best behavior — but Snoopy has landed on Santa’s naughty list. With just 12 days until Christmas, he sets out to prove he’s not such a bad beagle after all, discovering along the way that the season is about more than gifts.

Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc (Jude Hill), a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake (Chris Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah (Linda Cardellini). To help Marc defend himself, Jake devises an ambitious program he calls “Operation Warrior Kid” based on his SEAL training. Instead of teaching his nephew how to fight, Jake shows Marc what real courage is, facing down his own demons along the way. Based on the bestselling novel by former Navy SEAL Jocko Willink, “Way of the Warrior Kid” is directed by McG (“Charlie’s Angels,” “Terminator Salvation”) from a screenplay by Will Staples (“Without Remorse,” “The Right Stuff”).

Apple TV will also debut new episodes in November for the following currently airing shows:

Which of Apple TV’s November releases are you looking forward to? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

#3298. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

#3296. CAA’s Bryan Lourd Insists AI’s “Future Must Be Built With Artists, Not At Their Expense” As Agency Weighs In On NYT Vs. OpenAI Battle

Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics

EXCLUSIVE: It may be time for Sam Altman to ask himself if he really wants Robert Di Niro bellowing “are you AI scraping me?” at him.

While there is no direct Taxi Driver reference in the amicus brief filed by CAA in the nearly two-year old consolidated copyright infringement battle between OpenAI and the New York Times, Ta-Nehisi Coates, a collection of Florida and Arkansas papers, The Intercept and other outlets, Altman may not want to push it.

All jokes and references to the classic flick from 1976, Oscar winner and CAA client De Niro put his signature on the October 20 filed brief from the uberagency and others to assert to Altman and OpenAI “that technical silence is not legal consent.” De Niro is joined by Ariana DeBose, Helen Mirren, Emma Thompson, Julia Roberts, Scarlett Johansson, Vince Gilligan, Rosario Dawson, Dan Levy, Anne Hathaway and more in his objection to his work being high-tech feasting fodder. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Agencies WME Signs 'SNL's Jeremy Culhane News Josh Hartnett, Emma Thompson, Sally Hawkins, Danny Huston, Robert Aramayo & Chloe Pirrie Join Elle Fanning & Julianne Moore In Rebecca Miller's 'Moonsong: A Life In Seven Verses' - AFM

It’s standoff on what looks be the primary fault line of post-modern media.

“This case is about far more than one newspaper or one technology company,” CAA chief Bryan Lourd told Deadline today. ‘It is about the fundamental relationship between technological progress and creative rights, and who determines the value of creative work, who decides how that work is used, and whether creators will share in the opportunities AI creates.”

Unsurprisingly backed by Donald Trump’s DOJ, OpenAI has been in a copyright clash with the Grey Lady and others over its digital sticky fingers when it comes to training the Elon Musk-co-founded tech company’s models. As they did when this all started in 2024 (which has proven to be a millennium in AI terms). OpenAI (who are poised for an IPO any quarter now) claims fair use, and declares they “view this principle as fair to creators, necessary for innovators, and critical for US competitiveness.”

Not so much, says the circumspect Lourd, leaning on the development and Implementation of licensing frameworks for the AI era.

“Those questions are being answered now, and that is why CAA and other members of our community are weighing in,” the CAA CEO and Co-Chairman states. We strongly believe in the promise of AI, but its future must be built with artists, not at their expense, and grounded in consent, control, and compensation.”

In that context, CAA have been quite pro-active, launching their CAA Vault and other AI focused initiatives in the past few years. They also recognize the pace of the tech and its expectations are in a race with institutional reality. “Cultural change happens a long time before political and legal change does,” CAA‘s Chief Compliance Officer and Deputy General Counsel Tammy Brandt told Deadline’s LA Law Summit back in September.

With SAG-AFTRA, Adobe and ABBA name drops, plus cameos by co-plaintiffs Cate Blancett and Steven Soderbergh, the filing from Bass, Berry & Sims PLC actually accuses OpenAI of being out of times with the tech and the times (pun intended BTW). Refuting Team Altman’s contention that making licencing deal is cost prohibitive at this point in the tech’s evolution, the CAA-led brief asserts “the mechanisms to manage multi-rightsholder transaction costs are not only well-established, but are being actively adapted for the AI era by leaders across both the creative and technology sectors.”

Long lawsuit short: “Licensing at scale is not inherently impossible.”

Taking the strength in numbers approach, the NYC based BB&S are representing not just CAA in this brief but also Human Consent Foundation, Music Artists Coalition, National Association of Voice Actors, Writer, Inc., Creators Coalition on Artificial Intelligence, Blanchett, Soderbergh, and Nick Hexum in this brief

To that, here is the full A-list group, which would be a dream film festival invite list under any other name, going to digital barricade:

Bette Midler, Musician, Actor, Producer and Author

Christian Vesper, Film and Television Executive and Producer

Dame Emma Thompson, Actor and Screenwriter

Dan Levy, Actor, Writer, Producer and Director

Dave Eggers, Writer, Editor and Publisher

Greg Berlanti, Director, Producer and Writer

Madonna, Singer, Songwriter, Producer and Actor

Olivia Wilde, Actor, Director, Writer and Producer

Rian Johnson, Director, Producer and Writer

Richard Louderback, Artist and Illustrator

Stan Lee Foundation, Public Charity Dedicated to Literacy and the Narrative Arts

Vince Gilligan, Writer, Producer and Director

In a case that has been picking up traction in recent weeks, the NYT vs OpenAI conflict saw fellow mega-agency WME weigh in too last week. In a very similar tone to CAA’s submission, the Ari Emanuel-chaired company’s brief said WME “advocates that all uses of AI must be ethical and responsible, and any use of AI that affects talents’ and creators’ rights must come with proper compensation and authorization.”

The ongoing case had previously seen Game of Thrones overlord George R.R. Martin, John Grisham, Sarah Silverman, Bosch creator Michael Connelly, Jonathan Franzen, Jodi Picoult and more offer their take (Hint – not into AI using their work without paying for it). SAG-AFTRA, the American Federation of Musicians and the Writers Guild of America East and West filed their own joint brief on October 29 calling out OpenAI for “appropriating the work of middle- and working-class people to develop their technology.”

#3295. iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad

iPadOS 27.2 launched last week with a variety of new features for iPad, including a convenient change for multitasking.

When iPhone Duo first got into users’ hands, several reviews mentioned how the new Split View system felt more intuitive than iPadOS multitasking ever has.

And in iPadOS 27.2, there’s a convenient new multitasking change that’s likely inspired by iPhone Duo.

Apple hasn’t brought over the entire iOS system to the iPad. But it has made one common multitasking feature easier to set up: Split View.

From the official iPadOS 27.2 release notes:

Side-by-side multitasking is easier to set up with the option to choose a second app whenever you tile apps to the left or right with the window controls or menu bar

Starting with iPadOS 26 last year, setting up two apps side-by-side could fairly cumbersome.

You needed to open the first app, resize it, then swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see your other apps, select one, and in many cases manually resize the second app too.

But in iPadOS 27.2, any time you use Apple’s window resizing controls to tile an app left or right, you’ll immediately see the Home Screen and be able to tile a second app with a single tap.

FTA: "Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side."

Ok, great, but…then no one lists these keyboard shortcuts. Sure would have been helpful to paste them in here when talking about new features.

It’s not identical to the iPhone Duo experience, but it’s a lot closer to it than the old system was.

Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side.

#3294. The Newest 4K Amazon Fire TV Stick Is Nearly 60% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $15. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. You can also use Alexa to search for shows, launch apps, or control compatible smart home devices. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $25.

#3292. Paul W.S. Anderson Sets Film Adaptations Of Kevin J. Anderson Books ‘Nether Station’ & ‘Nether Vortex’

EXCLUSIVE: Paul W.S. Anderson, the filmmaker known for his work on six Resident Evil films, is set to direct Nether Station and Nether Vortex, film adaptations of the sci-fi horror books from bestselling author Kevin J. Anderson.

The novels follow Cammie Skoura, a brilliant, neurodivergent young scientist aboard a deep-space expedition that uncovers a trail of ancient ruins and long-dead alien civilizations leading toward a mind-shattering discovery. Cammie is described as a character the vein of Beth Harmon, Anya Taylor-Joy’s chess prodigy from the hit Netflix series The Queen’s Gambit. She anchors a story that fuses space exploration with the cosmic dread Weird Tales has published since its founding in 1923. Related Stories News Paul W.S. Anderson, Jeremy Bolt Plot Sega's 'The House Of The Dead' Movie: Exclusive Concept Art Acquisitions Vertical Acquires Paul W.S. Anderson's Fantasy Actioner 'In The Lost Lands' Starring Milla Jovovich & Dave Bautista

For W.S. Anderson, the duology marks a return to the cosmic horror genre that he explored early in his career with Event Horizon, the 1997 Paramount film starring Laurence Fishburne, Sam Neill, Kathleen Quinlan and Joely Richardson. Notably, author Anderson has cited that title as a direct influence on Nether Station. He released Nether Vortex via Blackstone Publishing’s imprint Weird Tales Presents on October 27, three years after Nether Station. Watch on Deadline

“Space is scary—think of how terrifying it would be all alone out in the cold, dark, oblivion?” Anderson said of the inspiration behind his books. “I tried to put all my fears and paranoia into Nether Station, and powerful films like Event Horizon were extremely influential in the writing. I couldn’t imagine a better director for this project than Paul W.S. Anderson.”

Jonathan Wakeham, a screenwriter with credits like Midas Man, To Catch a Killer and TNT limited series High Value Target: The Hunt for Saddam, will adapt the screenplays for the two films. W.S. Anderson will produce both alongside Jeremy Bolt (Event Horizon, Death Race), Weird Tales President John Harlacher and Weird Tales VP of film Tony Eldridge (The Equalizer franchise).

The filmmaker told us, “I’ve been a long term fan of Kevin’s work and to say it is cinematic is an understatement. I was thrilled to read Nether Station, the galleys of its sequel and also talk in detail with him about how he plans to expand the terrifying universe that he is creating. Lovecraftian cosmic horror, as experienced by a unique, young central character in Cammie Skoura, has all the ingredients for an unbelievably compelling and terrifying cinema experience.”

As a director, W.S. Anderson is coming off In the Lost Lands, a post-apocalyptic actioner starring his longtime Resident Evil lead Mila Jovovich, alongside Dave Bautista. He is repped by Ken Kamins of Key Creatives.

Kevin J. Anderson’s past activity in film & TV includes serving as co-producer on both Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Two and HBO Max’s Dune: Prophecy. This came about after co-writing a number of prequels and sequels to Frank Herbert’s sci-fi masterwork Dune alongside the author’s son, Brian Herbert. He is repped by Zero Gravity Management and Weintraub Tobin Chediak.

Wakeham is repped by Independent Talent Group and Lit Entertainment Group, whose Adam Kolbrenner also reps Weird Tales, alongside Brittney Brunelle and Lesley Sabga at The Seymour Agency.

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

Just get MagSafe going for iPads and create a base for it to attach to plus a HomeView like interface that turns on when attached.

Obviously though Apple wants an exclusive device because adding MagSafe to iPads would allow anyone to make such a base.

And if someone else comes up with an iPad solution it’ll likely get blocked from the App Store.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

Pricing is expected to be “around $1,000” per the report, but it may cost more depending on market prices for components. Tilley spoke to several former employees who said they expect Apple to use ‘HomeView Ultra’ branding for the product. As we’ve seen this fall though, Apple has been hesitant to expand its slate of Ultra products.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”

EXCLUSIVE: Disrupt Entertainment has acquired all North American distribution rights to North African superhero picture Atoman ahead of an international sales push for the film at the AFM.

The Pennsylvania-based company is gearing up to rollout the picture theatrically on at least 100 screens in early 2027 through AMC Theatres and other exhibitors.

The sci-fi adventure stars French Moroccan singer, rapper and Lartiste (Youssef Akdim) alongside French actor Samy Naceri, star of the Taxi franchise, who also shared the Cannes Best Actor award with the ensemble cast of Days of Glory in 2006, as well as Sarah Perles (Sofia), and Doudou Masto (The Horde). Related Stories Casting 'Slow Horses' Star Hiba Bennani To Star In Moroccan Drama 'Rass Jbel' Opposite Asaad Bouab News Mad Distribution Takes MENA Rights For Boundary-Pushing Moroccan Thriller 'Behind The Palm Trees' - Marrakech

Disrupt Entertainment is producing new English language dubs with human actors providing the voices. Watch on Deadline

Billed as North Africa’s first homegrown superhero franchise, Atoman world premiered at the Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival (BIFFF) in 2025.

Lartiste plays Hakim, an internationally renowned hacker who discovers he is a descendant of the ancient Atlanteans. When a world-destroying Astrolabe is uncovered in the Atlas Mountains, Hakim must tap into his newly discovered superhuman heritage to thwart global disaster.

Filmed entirely in North Africa, the groundbreaking film was spearheaded by director-producer Anouar Moatassim (Infiltrated).

It features a soundtrack and original score by Moroccan DJ Van combining pounding electronic rhythms, sweeping cinematic themes and contemporary North African musical influences, as well as tracks by internationally acclaimed European and Canadian artists Soprano, Mennel and Benny Adam.

Adam’s viral song from the film ‘Mok Ya Mok’ garnered millions of views and listens on the radio, online and on TikTok in 2026.

Following its world premiere at BIFFF in Brussels, the film had a limited theatrical release in France and a two-week run in Amazon France’s Top 5.

“My team and I are so happy to bring this incredible film to North American audiences,” said Disrupt Entertainment founding head Ben Yennie.

“Anouar Mutassim has created a visual masterwork that fuses high-stakes, blockbuster-caliber sci-fi action with an authentic cultural identity. This is exactly the kind of movie that brings message to the madness of genre filmmaking Disrupt was founded to amplify.”

The deal was brokered by Yennie and Alan Green of OneTwoThree Media, who will head to the AFM later this month with the film.

“Bringing Atoman to life was about proving that North Africa can deliver a globally competitive superhero story rooted in our own culture and mythology,” said Moatassim. “Disrupt Entertainment shares our passion, and both their creation of English language dubs and their large theatrical commitment for early 2027 is the perfect launchpad as we head into the energy of AFM.”

Atoman is produced by Moatassim and Aicha Kraus under their Casablanca Pictures banner. Yennie, alongside Bruce Nash of TheNumbers.com, coordinated completion funding for the film in 2025.

Amazon has knocked $100 off the latest Google Pixel Watch 5 (45mm, LTE), bringing it down to $429.99 from $529.99, its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. PCMag calls the Pixel Watch 5 the best smartwatch for Android users, largely because Gemini is built in so deeply—the assistant works proactively, so it can surface your flight details on the way to the airport or suggest a contact's number while you text about dinner plans, and a new AI-powered Health Coach reviews your workouts with tailored feedback, though some of its fitness advice sits behind a paid subscription.

#3287. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3284. You Can Get Microsoft Visual Studio Pro 2026 on Sale for Just $30 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

Half an hour after today’s closing bell, Apple will report its earnings for the fourth fiscal quarter of 2026, followed by a conference call where Apple CEO John Ternus and CFO Kevan Parekh will discuss the results.

This will be Ternus’s first earnings call since taking over from Tim Cook in September, and the conversation will likely center on how Apple navigated another quarter of memory shortages and rising component costs, as well as how it expects those challenges to affect its performance going into the holiday season.

During its previous earnings call, Apple projected revenue growth of between 9% and 11% year over year, despite significantly greater supply constraints affecting the iPhone, Mac, and iPad. If that forecast holds, quarterly revenue should come in between $111.69 billion and $113.74 billion.

The results will include just a few days of sales of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which launched on September 18. However, analysts will likely be particularly interested in Apple’s outlook for the current quarter, which includes the launch of the iPhone Duo, the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, and the HomeView smart home hub.

Apple’s conference call is scheduled to start at 2:00 p.m. PT / 5:00 p.m. ET, with the executives delivering prepared remarks before turning to analyst questions.

As usual, the call is set to be broadcast live, and you can listen in via ⁠Apple’s Investor Relations website.

#3280. Steve Ellis Dies: “Everlasting Love” Singer Was 76

Steve Ellis, singer for the British pop band Love Affair best known for the 1967 hit “Everlasting Love,” died October 30, of complications from a chronic illness. He was 76.

His death was announced on his Facebook page. Ellis lived in Brighton, England, and the family statement notes that he passed peacefully in the presence of loved ones.

Although never a major cultural presence in the United States, Ellis’ band Love Affair had several hits in the UK during the late 1960s and early ’70s in addition to their signature tune “Everlasting Love.” It was a cover of the Robert Knight song that features the memorable chorus “Open up your eyes, then you realize/Here I stand with my everlasting love.”

Watch the music video for the song below.

The Love Affair version went to No. 1 in the UK but failed to chart in the United States. A 1974 cover by Carl Carlton would have the most Stateside success.It appeared in two films: American Psycho in 2000 and in trailers for the 2021 Jamie Dornan film Belfast (Dornan himself performs the song in the actual film).

The Love Affair version caused a stir in the UK shortly after its release when it was revealed that, except for Ellis’ distinctive vocals, the instrumentation had been supplied by session musicians. In addition to Ellis, Love Affair consisted of keyboardist Lynton Guest, guitarist Rex Brayley, drummer Maurice Bacon and bassist Mick Jackson.

While “Everlasting Love” remains the band’s signature tune, other it had three other Top 10 UK singles in 1968-69 with “Rainbow Valley,” “A Day Without Love” and “Bringing on Back the Good Times.” “One Road” reached the Top 20. Ellis left for a solo career in 1969 and continued to record and perform for decades, often with reconstituted versions of Love Affair.

Born Stephen John Ellis in Edgware, Middlesex, on April 7, 1950, Ellis revealed in a Facebook post last year that he was withdrawing from a planned tour due to health issues. “I have never fully recovered from Covid in 2020 and chronic symptoms since have compromised my ability to sustain lengthy touring anymore,” he wrote.

Here's what to do if your Apple Watch failed to 'fall back'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With this weekend’s fall-back time change, your Apple Watch should’ve automatically updated to the correct time without intervention. But what if that’s not the case?

According to Apple, a bug is causing some Apple Watches to display the wrong time — off by an hour — on the home screen. While this hiccup doesn’t appear terribly widespread, it could not doubt lead to confusion, especially if you use your Apple Watch as an alarm clock.

Fortunately, there are two very easy ways to correct the issue if your Apple Watch is showing the wrong time. The first involves simply restarting your watch by holding down the side button until the slider appears, and then again until the Apple logo reappears.

However, if that doesn’t work, try the old watch face swaperoo trick — listed out in five easy steps below — for a surefire fix.

Read on to see full illustrated instructions for each step.

If your Apple Watch is showing the incorrect time by default, the first thing you'll want to do is open the Apple Watch app on your iPhone and tap on the "Face Gallery" at the bottom center of the screen.

Next, choose any of the watch faces by tapping "Get." We're only switching to this watch face temporarily, so it really doesn't matter which one you choose.

Once it's downloaded to your phone (this should take just a few seconds), tap on the preview of the new watch face, and then tap "Add to Watch" to temporarily install the face.

With the new watch face installed, your Apple Watch should now be showing the correct time, which means it is time to revert back to your original watch face. To do this, tap on "My Watch" at the bottom left of the screen to return to the Apple Watch app's main screen. Next, tap on your preferred watch face from the "My Faces" carousel at the top.

Finally, scroll down to the bottom of the watch face customization page and tap "Set as current Watch Face." This will reinstall your original watch face.

And just like that, your preferred Apple Watch face should be showing the correct daylight-savings-adjusted time.

#3275. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3272. MagSafe Monday: Pelican’s MagSafe Battery Pack is the battery built to go anywhere

A few weeks ago, I wrote about why the Pelican MagSafe Wallet is my favorite wallet for the fall, and the short version was that it’s built for being out and about. The Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack is the exact same idea applied to a power bank: a 5,000mAh MagSafe battery wrapped in a hardshell that’s meant to tossed around,

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Most MagSafe batteries are built for knowledge worker travel. Smooth plastic, a glossy finishe, and a body that picks up scratches the first time it shares a pocket with your keys, AirPods, etc. Pelican has been making cases for cameras and gear that survive the back of a truck for a long time, and their MagSafe pack carries that over. The hardshell exterior is designed to handle bumps and scratches, and the battery inside is protected rather than the thing doing the protecting.

For hiking, a day at the park, a camping trip, or a weekend of yard work with an audiobook going, this is the right trade-off.

The Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack is 5,000mAh, which is about one full charge for a standard iPhone and a solid top-up for a Pro Max. It charges via MagSafe at up to 15 watts, and the magnets are strong enough to stay put while the phone is in a jacket pocket or clipped to a backpack strap. It also works with any Qi device, so AirPods or a Samsung phone with a magnetic case will charge on it.

There’s a USB-C port for anything without MagSafe, with USB output and a short cable in the box. Four LEDs on the side show its remaining charge, which is still the simplest way to know whether to grab the battery or the wall charger before you walk out the door.

Two things to know going in. This is a 15-watt battery, not a Qi2.2 25-watt model, so it won’t match the fast-charging speeds you’ll see on the newer MagSafe batteries. For an outdoor MagSafe battery that spends most of its time topping up an iPhone in a pocket, I don’t think that matters much. The bigger one is the recharge speed. #3271. Netflix Orders ‘Prep’ YA Series Based On Book From ‘One Day’ EP Nicole Taylor & Gloria Sanchez Prods.

EXCLUSIVE: Netflix is turning to a 2005 book in search for its next YA hit. The streamer has given a straight-to-series order to Prep, an adaptation of Curtis Sittenfeld’s bestselling debut novel. The half-hour project, which had been developed internally, comes from Nicole Taylor, head writer and executive producer of Netflix’s limited series One Day — also based on a popular book — and Gloria Sanchez Productions.

Prep is a coming-of-age story about scholarship girl Lee Fiora’s high school years at Ault, a prestigious New England boarding school, and her journey to navigate friendship, crushes and class as a fish out of water among her privileged, confident classmates. Related Stories News Jason Statham & Guy Ritchie Reunite For Netflix Feature 'Dogfight' News Zoe Kazan's 'East Of Eden' Adaptation Manifests Audience Growth Comparable To 'Adolescence' -- Here's How It Happened

BAFTA TV Award winner Taylor is writer and showrunner. She executive produces with Will Ferrell, Jessica Elbaum, and Alix Taylor for Gloria Sanchez Productions and Sittenfeld. A writers room is slated to open in January. Watch on Deadline

“Prep is my all time favourite novel and I have longed to adapt it for the entire twenty years since I first read it and found myself reflected uncannily back,” Scottish native Taylor said. “There is no more acute depiction of the introspective, bookish self-conscious adolescent girl and no more truthful or excoriating take on the perils of social mobility than in Curtis Sittenfeld’s beautiful first novel. I am overjoyed to be adapting for Netflix.”

The series green light by Netflix comes almost 22 years after Prep was published by Random House in January 2005 and 10 years after HBO took a stab at adapting it as a comedy series from 30 Rock‘s Colleen McGuinness and Game of Thrones‘ Carolyn Strauss, which did not move forward. While utilizing a half-hour format, Netflix’s Prep is not a comedy. (Taylor’s drama One Day also had shorter episodes, ranging from 19 to 38 minutes each.)

“I’m overjoyed that Netflix is making Prep as a TV show — the 22-year wait was worth it!,” Sittenfeld said. “Alix Taylor at Gloria Sanchez has guided the project forward with such intelligence and enthusiasm, and Nicole Taylor’s scripts are truly brilliant. Nicole’s adaptation makes me understand my own novel, and myself, better. My 51-year-old self can’t wait to see what they do with this story of privilege, longing, and teen angst.”

Prep joins Netflix’s slate of upcoming YA series that includes The Sticks, The Body, Poser, and Sid & Zoey. Since Since H1 2023 when Netflix began releasing comprehensive viewership information, YA titles have generated over 10.4B global views on the streamer, with two of them, Wednesday and Stranger Things, occupying four spots on Netflix’s Top 10 most popular English-language series list, #1, #3, #4 and #6.

Taylor won a BAFTA TV Award for her three-part BBC series Three Girls. She also wrote the BBC miniseries The Nest and the movie Wild Rose starring Jessie Buckley, the latter of which she adapted to the stage, with an off-Broadway production opening later this month. Taylor is repped by UTA, Curtis Brown Group, and Ziffren Brittenham.

Sittenfeld’s other novels include Romantic Comedy, which is being adapted as a movie by New Line and Hello Sunshine; Rodham, which was previously in development as a TV series at Hulu; The Man of My Dreams; American Wife; Sisterland and Eligible. She is repped by WME.

#3269. iOS 27.2’s clever new Messages feature can be tailored to your needs

iOS 27.2 launched last week with a convenient new Messages feature called ‘Suggested Actions.’ Here’s how you can customize the feature to your liking.

If your iPhone is running iOS 27.2, you might have noticed a handy addition in the Messages app.

Whenever a message contains actionable information—an event you might want to add to your calendar, or todo you need reminding of—Messages will add a ‘Suggested Action’ right below the relevant message.

Using these new suggestions, with a quick tap you can turn the message into an action. And they’re so small and unobtrusive in the UI that they don’t clutter up the app at all.

But depending on your needs, you might want to enable or disable some of these suggestions. And Apple lets you do that with a surprising level of granularity.

Inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages -> Suggested Actions you’ll find customization options for the feature.

There are five different types of suggestions that can be enabled or disabled in Settings. By default, all five are enabled.

I’m planning to leave all five enabled, because I’ve found the feature a useful addition. But it’s great to see Apple offer a refreshing level of control like this right off the bat.

Note: Suggested Actions are powered by Apple Intelligence, so you’ll need an AI-compatible iPhone to get the feature.

What do you think of Messages’ new feature in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

If you want to get your hands on an iPhone Duo, you've got a long wait ahead of you. Current iPhone Duo wait times stretch to the end of the year and into January, depending on where you order from. The question on everyone's mind is when the supply issue is going to be fixed, and the current answer is... that we have no idea.

In fact, Apple CEO John Ternus doesn't really have an answer for that question, either. Speaking to Reuters, following Apple's latest earnings report, Apple's new head honcho admitted the company can't make any sort of predictions.

"Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible," Ternus said. "But at this point, we're not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance."

Obviously, when the CEO of the company can't comment on supply issues, you know the situation is pretty bad. Though whether it's because Ternus really doesn't know when supply and demand will equalize, or because he simply doesn't want to make any promises that may not be kept, isn't clear.

Apple did seem surprised that the iPhone Duo has been in such high demand, and it's possible that the company is simply being overly cautious. Because there's little point in getting hopes up until Apple can be sure Duo shortages have a firm end date.

It certainly doesn't help that scalpers seem to be trying to snatch up the iPhone Duo to sell on at a premium. As is the case with a lot of in-demand items, scalpers have been employing bots to grab as much stock as they can, including any Duo units that become available for in-store pickup.

In other words, trying to pick up an iPhone Duo before the end of the year is effectively a losing battle. You're far better off trying to be patient and ordering through one of the major carriers and retailers. Wait times are already stretching into January at most retailers, and it doesn't sound like things are going to get better.
