#3246. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

#3245. Apple forecasts its biggest revenue quarter ever despite supply constraints

During today’s earnings call following its fiscal Q4 2026 report, Apple said it expects its December quarter “to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company.” Here are the details.

Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with revenue climbing 12% year over year to $114.5 billion and net profit reaching $30.71 billion. This marked September-quarter records on both fronts, despite supply constraints on iPhone, Mac, and iPad, as well as rising memory costs.

During the conference call following the earnings report, Apple acknowledged that higher memory costs were putting pressure on its profit margins, while also warning of limited supply-chain flexibility, stronger-than-expected demand for Mac and iPad, and ongoing shortages of the new iPhone Duo.

Still, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh was very clear about what the company expects from the next fiscal quarter, which includes the holiday shopping season:

We expect our December quarter total company revenue to grow between 7 and 10% year over year, which reflects our best view of constrained supply. We expect this to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company.

If this pans out, Apple’s fiscal Q1 2027 revenue should fall between $153.82 billion and $158.13 billion, adding between $10 billion and $14.4 billion in revenue compared to the year-ago quarter.

Beyond revenue, Parekh also shared Apple’s expectations for several other financial metrics during the December quarter:

Parekh noted that “third-party licensing and foreign exchange” will be the primary headwinds for the Services revenue, while higher memory costs and “some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI” are expected to put further pressure on the company’s gross margins.

Finally, Apple cautioned that its outlook “assumes that global tariff rates, policies, and their application remain in effect as of this call, and the global macroeconomic outlook does not worsen from today.“

#3244. Living with Mom and trading on margin. The regular investor gets in on Wall Street's record stock borrowing binge

HOUSTON — During a late night at home in May 2021, Hy Luu, a 29-year-old engineering consultant, was researching how to obtain more capital to invest in shares of Tesla.

That's when he discovered margin investing: the act of borrowing money from a broker to buy securities such as stocks, while using existing investments as collateral. Borrowing would give him more buying power, and he could pay it back as the stock appreciated. The main risk would be a margin call, or having to deposit more money into the account, if its value fell.

It was all too good to be true, Luu thought.

Luu — who lives with his mother, Kim Nguyen, in a three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in Houston — decided to get her opinion on the topic, given that she used to work as an accountant and just so happened to still be awake that evening. The 66-year-old retiree found it interesting.

That was the reassurance he needed, and it wasn't long before he started using margin to invest in Tesla for the first time. A year or so later, he had amassed more than $100,000 of margin debt.

"I went really crazy," he told CNBC in an interview. "The stock was going up, and so I was like, 'There's no way I could lose.'"

After five years of margin investing — including a period in 2022 where he worried that further declines in Tesla could trigger a margin call — Luu is working to pay down his largest margin balance ever. In June, he exercised $165,000 on five Tesla call options and bought 500 shares at $330 per share. After accounting for the cash in his account, this drove his borrowing to more than $156,000.

Tesla swung from below $370 a share to more than $430 during that month.

Between his Tesla investments, his company stock and 401(k) — while subtracting his margin debt as well as other debt he's accumulated, such as his car loan and student loans — Luu's net worth has skyrocketed to more than $800,000 from negative territory seven years ago.

"I'm very close to becoming a millionaire," the investor said. He did stress, "What I'm doing is risky. I don't recommend anyone do it."

Yet, Luu has found himself part of a growing trend taking hold in the market.

Retail investors like Luu are borrowing more and more money to invest. Robinhood's margin book grew to a record $21.6 billion in the second quarter, up 127% year over year and a 332% increase from the $5 billion seen in Q2 2024. To margin invest on the platform, eligible users must have a portfolio value of at least $2,000.

"Robinhood has made a really concerted effort to go after customers that are actively using margin because they're the most active traders," said Devin Ryan, head of financial technology research at Citizens.

Brokerage firms can benefit from margin investing by collecting interest on margin loans, while highly active customers can also generate additional trading-related revenue.

"If you look at the offers that Robinhood has had in the market over the past couple of years, it's been targeting those customers with obviously transfer bonuses, but also very low margin rates, very high yields on their cash," Ryan said.

To be sure, other parts of Robinhood's business are also growing, including retirement assets — which have nearly quadrupled in the last two years.

Another factor fueling the rise in margin investing is easier access through smartphones, according to Ryan.

"Having very little friction in investing and having everything at your fingertips, and then having a really seamless mobile experience where it's not clunky, I think, plays a big part of that," he said.

A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC its products are designed to appeal to a number of customers, saying that "we don't believe it's accurate to characterize" its transfer promotions as specifically targeting "active traders who are trading on margin or may trade on margin." The company said it tries to "meet users where they are," and they "reject any implication" that the company is "encouraging risky trading."

Robinhood's margin debt isn't the only one reaching records. Total margin debt hit an all-time high of around $1.5 trillion in June, per the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which incorporates data on both institutional investors such as hedge funds and retail investors.

Not all of that debt is driven by fresh borrowing due to new borrowing decisions. For example, as equities rise in value, an investor may need to cover a short position that's been marked to market, or valued at its current price.

Nonetheless, Sam Huszczo, chief investment officer at SGH Wealth Management, thinks the market's bull run — which has seen multiple record highs this year alone — is feeding a shift in investor psychology, and margin debt is one sign.

"That's greed," the founder said, adding that it's "not everywhere" in the market, but it's "certainly creeping into pockets."

"Margin, that's only the tip of the iceberg of what we can see," he continued. "Fear of missing out is just the emotion of jealousy with a brokerage account."

Huszczo considers the market to actually be "way healthier" than people think. Though he recognizes that increasing margin debt and the rise of risky assets such as leveraged ETFs inject more fragility in the system.

"People need to differentiate between what's a legitimate momentum growth investment and what's reckless chasing," Huszczo also said.

Huszczo shares the commonly held belief among financial advisors that investors' portfolios shouldn't be overly concentrated in one stock or even one sector.

Yet Luu has been zeroed in on Tesla ever since he bought his first share in late 2019. Earlier that year, he had started his current job — a time when he knew nothing about investing, he said. It wasn't until a co-worker told him to download Robinhood months later that he began looking into stocks and other assets.

"I started making money, and I quickly learned, 'Now I'm making money, what do I do with it?'" he said. "I started investing in index funds and even in crypto, and then I did the math. I looked at the returns, and I was like, 'This is very slow returns. I'm never gonna reach retirement, financial independence until like 65.'"

Little did he know that a decision he had made that summer would become his guiding light.

"I was choosing between a Honda Civic and a Tesla Model 3, and my friend, he scheduled a test drive for me to drive the Model 3," Luu said. "My plan was only to go into it just to test drive it. I wasn't going to buy anything. I wasn't going to put in any reservation. Long story short, after the test drive, I put in my reservation the same day, and I got the car like two weeks later."

Seeing the value the car provides in his life, Luu said he can envision a future where electric and autonomous vehicles are commonplace. Because of how much he believes in that future, he considers Tesla the "easiest" investment he's made, and over the course of seven years of investing in the company, he has generally held his shares.

However, things got a bit more difficult with his strategy when Tesla shares began falling in 2022, putting him in the vulnerable position of potentially receiving a margin call. 2022 was Tesla's worst year on record, with the stock finishing off the year at $123.18 after a roughly 65% decline.

In search of more capital, Luu made a serious financial decision with his mother's approval.

"I refinanced the house to get access to an extra $30,000 of capital, and I used that to pay down my margin debt," he said.

Luu understands the level of risk that accompanies trading with margin. Because he's been using margin for most of the nearly seven years he's been investing in Tesla, he has deemed his investing strategy "gambling with an asterisk."

For now, it has paid off. In the last five years, Tesla shares have risen more than 43% to $375. However, the volatile stock is about 25% off of its all-time high near $499.

"It's very easy to see it as gambling, because obviously all your money is in one stock, and that's inherently risky," he said. "But the reason why I say there's nuance to it is because it's a matter of investing temperament, financial discipline and time horizon."

With a time horizon of "many decades," a temperament he labels as "very calm and collected" and a "very high" conviction in Tesla, Luu believes he's "at no risk of panic selling," even when the market tanks.

Still, the situation points out another danger: Missing an opportunity to make an investment when an equity is undervalued. When Luu was scrambling to raise funds to meet his margin obligation, it reduced his flexibility to purchase more Tesla shares at the lower price.

Margin levels this high have been followed by risk-off periods in equities.

Whenever monthly margin debt has grown above 45% year over year since 1960, there were declines in the stock market five out of six times, data from Fundstrat Global Advisors shows. June's margin debt record came in at 49%, but the S&P 500 has still added more than 13% in 2026. A swing into the red by year-end in accordance with this historic pattern would be a dramatic move — one that would be considered highly unusual for the stock market.

The firm also found that the median performance for S&P 500 forward returns following a breakout of 40% year-over-year margin debt growth has been worse off 12 months later as opposed to one month after it. To be exact, the S&P 500's median 12-month forward return is a 4.2% decline, while the median one-month return is a drop of 2.2%.

In essence, the more rapidly margin debt rises, the worse it is for S&P 500 returns over 12 months.

While margin debt doesn't necessarily cause S&P 500 declines, it can exacerbate existing moves to the downside if there's a significant amount of leverage in the market, said Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat.

"The premise of gains beget gains, it turns into losses beget losses, and that's what's troublesome," Singh said. "You have these losses, they keep piling up, and then the stock gets sold, and everyone's starting to close out their position, and it becomes this huge train wreck that's very hard to stop, and it adds a lot of volatility to the market."

Then again, Singh sees why investors like Luu are leaning into such a risky strategy. "No one ever got rich by diversifying," she said.

Luu, who said he's been a "hobbyist" from an early age, has folded in investing as one of his many hobbies, which include activities like climbing and playing guitar. It's become such a hobby that he's created his own social media account detailing his investing journey.

Even if Luu reaches his financial goals, he "wouldn't ever stop investing," he said. Instead, he said he "would probably start investing in SpaceX."

It's not just Luu who views trading as a hobby.

Fundstrat's Singh explained that American traders, particularly younger ones, feel they have to take bigger risks to get ahead. She said it's part of a broader trend dubbed financial nihilism, in which young investors grappling with a tough job market and high inflation turn to less-stable investing tools.

"It makes a lot of sense why individuals, specifically retail investors, keep gravitating towards this margin debt," the economic strategist added. "This is like a drug, and I think people just can't get enough of it in this economy."

Kevin Davis, a 59-year-old retail investor who made a living as a rapper in the 1980s and '90s before becoming a stock broker, believes the risks with leveraged trading outweigh the rewards.

"It's gambling. You're borrowing money you don't have, and so if it goes the other way, now you have a clock on your money, and it's ticking," said Davis, who owns an investing technology platform. "The market's not going to save you. It never does."

"Don't play the margin game," the Florida resident warned.

Luu became an engineering consultant because his father, who died of lung cancer in 2012, exposed him to computing. His mother said that between her two sons, Luu most resembles his father not only in terms of his features but also his character.

Reflecting on what her late husband might have thought about Luu's investing pursuits, Nguyen paused for a moment, holding a slight smile.

She then said, "He would've said he's proud of him."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito and Deena Zaidi contributed to this report.

#3243. Apple stock drops nearly 3% after hours following Q4 2026 results

Apple shares fell as much as 4.43% in after-hours trading on Monday during the company’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, before recovering some of those losses later in the evening. Here are the details.

Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with a 12% increase in revenue, another 12% increase in net profit, and record revenue from its Services category, following its first sequential quarterly decline in 15 quarters.

The results also included a 17% increase in iPhone revenue and a 24% increase in Mac revenue, but an 8% decline in Wearables, Home, and Accessories revenue, which Apple attributed to “a difficult compare against the launch of the Watch SE 3 and the AirPods Pro 3 in the prior year,” and a 10% decline in iPad revenue, which Apple attributed to supply constraints and a similarly difficult comparison against last year’s A16-powered iPad launch.

During the conference call, Apple CEO John Ternus, CFO Kevan Parekh, and COO Sabih Khan fielded questions from analysts about rising memory costs, recent hardware price increases, and ongoing supply constraints, including those affecting the iPhone Duo.

Hopefully Apple can use this aberration in trading algorithms to cancel as many shares as possible on the cheap!

The executives also offered a mixed outlook for the holiday quarter, with Apple expecting its highest quarterly revenue ever, but slower year-over-year growth, lower profit margins, and continued shortages of Mac and iPad models.

After ending the regular trading session down 1.83%, Apple shares initially climbed 0.5% to $340.00 following the earnings release. However, as the conference call progressed, the stock reversed course, falling to $323.33, or 4.43% below Monday’s closing price. Shares then recovered some of those losses, ending the after-hours session at $328.81, down 2.81%.

Of course, post-earnings after-hours trading doesn’t necessarily reflect how a stock will perform during the next day’s regular session, so it remains to be seen how investors will react when markets reopen on Tuesday after digesting tonight’s news.

#3242. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3240. Bosch gives chips their own division, eyeing €5bn in sales by 2030

The car-parts giant will open its fabs to outside customers and chase robotics demand from January 2028.

The Bosch Parkhaus near Stuttgart Airport

Bosch will move its semiconductor business into a dedicated division from January 2028, as the German supplier looks to expand chip sales beyond the automotive industry.

The company is targeting annual semiconductor revenue of around €5bn by 2030, it announced today. The new unit, which will be called Semiconductors, will remain part of Bosch rather than becoming a separate company.

Its chip business currently sits within the Mobility Electronics division, which will continue to handle the production of electronic control units for vehicles.

The restructuring reflects Bosch’s ambition to find more customers for its chips outside the automotive sector.

The company plans to open its manufacturing facilities to external clients and expand its foundry business, producing semiconductors for other companies.

Its target markets include robotics, factory automation and AI data centres, alongside consumer devices such as phones and wearables. Bosch says its components already play a role in controlling humanoid robots.

“With the founding of a dedicated unit, we are opening a new chapter in our more than 60-year semiconductor history,” said Erik Rein, who heads Bosch’s chip business.

Bosch has several established positions in specialised semiconductor markets. It is a leading supplier of MEMS sensors, the miniature motion and pressure sensors used in devices such as smartphones and robots.

The company also produces silicon carbide chips and custom circuits for power systems.

Its manufacturing footprint spans around 40 chip sites worldwide. Bosch has invested approximately €3bn in its wafer plants in Dresden and Reutlingen, and is spending around $2bn to convert its Roseville, California facility to silicon carbide production.

The company also plans to expand its test centre in Penang, Malaysia, through the mid-2030s. It holds a 10% stake in ESMC, the TSMC-led semiconductor joint venture building a factory in Dresden.

The move comes as Europe’s automotive industry continues to grapple with chip supply risks.

Carmakers spent part of the autumn managing shortages during the Nexperia dispute, which exposed the industry’s dependence on a limited number of suppliers.

By offering manufacturing capacity to outside customers, Bosch could help diversify Europe’s chip supply while seeking new markets for its own technology.

Bosch deputy chairman Markus Heyn said the company’s sensors are “the key” to its products and “the technological basis” for its customers’ innovations.

#3239. Apple recently notified users in 99 countries of potential mercenary spyware attacks

Apple reportedly sent notifications to users in 99 countries warning of potential mercenary spyware attacks, as German authorities investigate reports that lawmakers and government officials may have been targeted. Here are the details.

A couple of reports from The Financial Times and TechCrunch today offer complementary details about a new wave of Apple threat notifications warning users that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware.

As we’ve covered before, Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to users it believes may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks. The company doesn’t disclose who may be behind the attacks or confirm whether a device has been compromised, but advises recipients to take the warnings seriously and seek expert assistance.

You can learn more about Apple’s recommendations for protecting against mercenary spyware, including how to enable Lockdown Mode, here.

Back to today’s reports, The Financial Times says that German lawmakers and government officials began receiving threat notifications from Apple last Thursday, prompting the country’s Federal Office for Information Security to issue an urgent warning over the weekend.

The agency advised recipients to “assume their device is no longer secure,” while the German government said it was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously” and “working flat out to investigate the circumstances of the incident.”

The FT noted that German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius declined to say whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those affected, and added that the attacks reportedly exploited a “zero-click” vulnerability, allowing attackers to compromise devices without any interaction.

Knowledge of their targets’ phone numbers was all that the hackers needed to carry out the attack.

As it reported on the alerts, TechCrunch noted that “others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple,” including Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, who shared his alert on X.

It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries.

Mortada also noted in his tweet that he had previously been targeted by Pegasus spyware in 2017 and 2021, and that he does not know who was behind the latest attempt or whether it was connected to an investigative documentary he directed.

#3237. SCOTUS sets hearing date for Apple’s appeal in Epic Games case

The U.S. Supreme Court has officially scheduled oral arguments in Apple’s appeal in its long-running legal battle with Epic Games. Here are the details.

Back in 2020, Epic Games sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store for introducing an alternative in-app payment system through a remotely activated update.

The following year, despite ruling in Apple’s favor on nine of Epic’s ten claims, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled that Apple could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment options outside the App Store.

As a result, Apple changed its rules to allow external purchase links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on transactions completed through them, along with restrictions on how those links could be presented.

Epic challenged Apple’s implementation, and the district court agreed. In April 2025, Judge Rogers ordered Apple to remove those restrictions and stop charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store, finding the company in civil contempt for violating the original injunction.

Since then, Apple has allowed developers to direct users to external payment options in the US App Store without charging a commission, while continuing to challenge the contempt ruling.

After unsuccessful attempts before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, Apple eventually took its case to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to review whether Apple could be held in contempt for violating the “spirit” of an injunction, even when its text did not specifically prohibit the conduct in question.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only review the civil contempt ruling, not how much, if anything, Apple can charge developers for purchases made outside the App Store. That issue is being handled separately by the district court, after the Ninth Circuit overturned the blanket ban on commissions in December.

Earlier today, the Supreme Court’s official docket for the case was updated with a date for oral arguments.

According to the filing, Apple and Epic Games will present their arguments before the Supreme Court on Monday, January 11, 2027, though both sides have already outlined many of their arguments in recent filings.

In September, Apple filed its opening brief with the Supreme Court, arguing that the contempt ruling should be overturned because the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit it from charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store.

In its brief, Apple cited multiple court decisions to support its argument that a party cannot be held in civil contempt unless an injunction clearly prohibits the conduct in question.

A few days after Apple’s filing, the US Department of Justice and several legal and business groups also submitted briefs supporting at least part of the company’s argument.

The DOJ, however, also argued that the lower courts were right to hold Apple in contempt over some of its restrictions on external purchase links, including a requirement that developers use what Apple called “plain buttons,” which could not have contrasting backgrounds.

With the hearing now scheduled, the case is one step closer to a final decision from the Supreme Court. However, both sides still have some paperwork to submit before then, as Epic Games has until November 13 to file its brief responding to Apple’s arguments, while Apple’s reply is due December 14.

#3236. OpenAI hires former US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security

Dan Driscoll will advise on how AI can strengthen national and cyber security, with a focus on US allies. He left the Pentagon in September after months of tension with Pete Hegseth.

Dan Driscoll, then Secretary of the Army, in Ashgabat, Turkmenistan, in January 2026.

OpenAI has hired Dan Driscoll, the 26th Secretary of the US Army, the company said on Monday. He takes a new role: senior counselor for national security modernization.

Driscoll will advise on how advanced AI can strengthen national and cyber security. He will work with OpenAI’s leaders and outside partners. His main focus is helping US allies use the technology responsibly.

“National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years,” Driscoll said in a statement.

He said AI would help people in national security cut through paperwork. It would also help them make sense of more information and get answers faster.

Driscoll left the Pentagon in September after months of tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Gareth Vipers reported this for The Wall Street Journal. Driscoll is a former Army officer and a law-school classmate of Vice President JD Vance, the Journal reported.

As Army secretary, he oversaw nearly one million soldiers and more than 265,000 Army civilians, OpenAI said. Driscoll said he had also served as acting director of the ATF.

“The US has an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI,” said Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive.

Driscoll will also help OpenAI’s teams understand what national security institutions need. OpenAI said the hire builds on Daybreak, its cyber resilience programme with allies and partners.

OpenAI has opened Daybreak to Ukraine and pitched it to utilities in the US.

In February, OpenAI agreed to deploy its models on the Defense Department’s classified network. That came after rival Anthropic’s relationship with the Pentagon broke down, Rachel Metz reported for Bloomberg. Anthropic is still fighting its Pentagon case in court.

#3235. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3233. Apple earnings suggest the iPhone 18 launch strategy is really working

Yesterday’s AAPL earnings report revealed record revenue for a September quarter, and within it was an arguably even more significant record: iPhone revenue.

That’s because this year’s quarter only includes just two new iPhone models compared to the four released last year …

Apple reported fiscal quarter four revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year on year. Within that was iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion, which was also a quarterly record. What makes this significant is the year-on-year comparison, when you consider the new iPhone launch revenue included within each quarter.

(Although the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time, pre-orders didn’t open until October, so none of this revenue is included in Apple’s fiscal Q4.)

The main thing that changed this year is that Apple didn’t launch a base model iPhone 18 alongside the Pro models: that launch won’t happen until early next year. The biggest factor in this decision was likely component shortages, Apple wanting to ensure that it could fulfill demand for premium models, but the revenue figures suggest that the timings also influenced purchase decisions.

Many people upgrade their iPhones on a fixed cycle, be that every one, two, or three years – and that cycle begins each September. When upgrade time rolled around and there was no base model iPhone 18 available, it seems likely that a significant number of those who would have bought it decided to instead opt for the iPhone 18 Pro rather than wait.

That may suggest rather modest sales of the base model iPhone 18 when it rolls around, but if Apple managed to persuade a significant number of would-be buyers to opt for a more expensive model, the company won’t be shedding any tears about that.

Of course, there are a couple of other factors in the mix here. First, the iPhone 17 proved extremely popular and remains on sale today, so it will have contributed something to this year’s Q4 revenue. Second, Apple cited revenue rather than profit, and the $100 price increase for this year’s Pro models will played a role. But overall I do think it paints a very encouraging picture for this split launch strategy.

What’s your take? Do you think it reflects well on iPhone 18 Pro sales, or do you think it can be explained away by the price increase and continuing popularity of the iPhone 17? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
